item.title: NFL Thursday Night Football preview: Bills open their new stadium with a great matchup vs. Lions
item.description: Josh Allen and the Bills are coming off an impressive win at Houston.
item.content:encoded:
The Buffalo Bills have been around since 1960 and they have played in only two home stadiums.

War Memorial Stadium was their home through the 1972 season, but the team quickly outgrew it. Then came Rich Stadium, which would undergo a few name changes that included Ralph Wilson Stadium and Highmark Stadium. There were 429 games and many great memories there. But eventually the Bills had to upgrade from that stadium too.

The Bills had one of the more outdated stadiums in the NFL. That's not the case anymore. New Highmark Stadium cost $2.2 billion and has its first regular-season game Thursday night against the Detroit Lions. While there have been complaints about obstructed views at some of the seats, overall the stadium looked luxurious during the preseason.

And Bills fans have a pretty good team residing in the new stadium.

The Bills are coming off a thrilling 36-31 win in Week 1 over the Houston Texans in which quarterback Josh Allen played a remarkable game, including a game-winning touchdown in the final two minutes. Allen is an MVP favorite and the Bills are a Super Bowl contender. Add on the excitement over the new stadium, and it's a good time to be a Bills fan.

The regular-season opener in new Highmark Stadium should be a lot of fun. The Lions are a good and exciting team as well. While their Week 1 overtime win over the New Orleans Saints was closer than they'd hoped, especially after taking a 21-0 lead, they escaped with a win and have high hopes for the season. It's a team that won 15 games two seasons ago and still has most of the stars from that squad. There are some questions about an injured Lions secondary, which might just mean we see a lot of touchdowns.

One way or another, it will be a memorable night for the Bills franchise.

Who needs it more?

We could break it down in football terms here, but only one team has history at stake. You don't want to follow the pomp and circumstance of opening a new stadium with a loss. Nobody in Michigan will remember years from now if the Lions won a Week 2 game against an AFC team. But Bills fans will recall what happened in the first regular-season game at new Highmark Stadium (for the record, they won their first game at their previous stadium 9-7 over the New York Jets in 1973). There will be pressure on the Bills given the importance of the night in Western New York. Whatever happens will be part of the stadium's history.

Key player: Lions WR Jameson Williams

Williams has established himself as a very good receiver but he's coming off a poor Week 1. Williams had multiple drops, though it didn't ultimately cost Detroit as the Lions went on to win 31-30 in overtime. Williams has had issues with drops through his career, but Detroit probably can't afford more if they want to beat the Bills. The Lions' offense is incredibly condensed: Jahmyr Gibbs, Amon-Ra St. Brown, Sam LaPorta and Williams accounted for 53 of 57 touches among skill position players in Week 1. They need all of those players at their best to beat a Bills team that is going to put up plenty of points. Williams can help keep Detroit in the game with a few big plays.

Betting market watch, by Ben Fawkes

This line has been on the move. The lookahead was Bills -3, it re-opened on Sunday night at -3.5 and it's now as high as Bills -5.5 at some sportsbooks. The total has also ticked up from 52.5 to 54.5, both because of how good each team's offense looked in Week 1 ... and how bad each team's defense played. With Josh Allen and Co. opening Highmark Stadium in Buffalo, it's going to be a tall task for the Lions to stay in this game if its secondary doesn't play better. The betting public is backing Buffalo to cover, and while I don't hate the pick, I'd target the Bills' team total instead. If Tyler Shough had 410 yards passing and led the Saints to 29 first downs (8-of-17 on third down), what will Allen do against Detroit's D?

Check out more of Ben's work at the Yahoo Sports betting hub.

Fantasy football storylines, by Scott Pianowski

The total is set in the 55 range for Bills and Lions tonight, so it's a juicy spot for fantasy managers. Here are three stories I'll have my eyes on.

1. Can this be D.J. Moore's dream season? Although Moore was a target hog in Carolina and had one great year in Chicago, he's never gone past eight touchdowns in a season. Hopes are especially high for Moore in Buffalo after a 5-100-1 opener, and the Detroit secondary is ravaged by injury.

2. Will Jameson Williams bounce back? Williams left a bunch of points on the field last week, struggling with drops and focus. Given that he had nine targets and one running play called for him (botched by his hands), just 45 yards goes down as a disappointment. But the Lions have a narrow target tree, and Williams can score from anywhere on the field.

3. Can Dalton Kincaid keep the heavy usage? Kincaid was limited to 38% snaps last year, as the Bills helped him manage knee issues. He ran on 72% of the snaps in last week's opener, helping him produce a 5-130-0 line. Perhaps the timing is right for his breakout year.

item.title: NFL Injury Report, Week 2: Latest news updates, fantasy football analysis
item.description: We're updating you on the latest NFL injuries for Week 2 to help with your fantasy football lineups.
item.content:encoded:
It's always tough navigating that first injury report coming out of preseason and training camp. Some injuries are downplayed and others weren't as serious as initially thought. We also get some surprises (we're looking at you Raiders and Brock Bowers).

But we've gotten through most of the action for Week 1 and can look ahead to which injuries we'll need to track going into the second slate of the season. Below is all the latest news and updates, plus some fantasy football analysis to help with weekly lineup tinkering.

NFL Injury Report, Week 2

Quarterback

  • Kyler Murray, MIN (concussion)

  • Sam Darnold, SEA (hip — OUT for Week 2)

  • Michael Penix Jr., ATL (knee)

  • Tua Tagovailoa, ATL (oblique)

  • Joe Burrow, CIN (back)

Murray: It was a tough Minnesota debut for Murray, exiting early in the contest after a questionable hit from Packers S Javon Bullard. Prior to the hit, Murray had thrown an egregious interception into triple coverage. Murray did not return, finishing the game 3-for-5 for 18 yards and the INT, plus two carries for nine yards. He's in the concussion protocol, and if he's not cleared by Week 2, it'll be Carson Wentz again for the Vikings, which actually isn't bad news for Justin Jefferson.

Darnold: Don't forget about the reigning Super Bowl champ. Darnold exited the opener early Wednesday and will miss Week 2. He could return as soon as Week 3, but will likely avoid going on IR. Drew Lock played well enough in relief to help Jaxon Smith-Njigba maintain elite status. The Cardinals are an easier matchup than the Pats, as well. Lock isn't a fantasy consideration outside of a desperation play in deep 2-QB formats.

Running Back

  • TreVeyon Henderson, NE (ankle) — FP at practice

  • Dylan Sampson, CLE (knee)

  • Alvin Kamara, NO (knee)

  • Jordan Mason, MIN (thumb — IR)

  • D'Andre Swift, CHI (ankle) — LP at practice

  • Kyle Monangai, CHI (hamstring) — LP at practice

  • RJ Harvey, DEN (hamstring) — LP at practice

Mason: Mason's thumb injury, suffered in the Vikings' loss against the Packers, was more serious than initially though, as the team placed the running back on IR on Wednesday. They signed DeeJay Dallas off the practice squad, but we should expect to see a lot more of veteran Aaron Jones Sr. out of the Minnesota backfield; he just might end up being a huge draft value. We could also see what rookie Demond Claiborne is capable of, now that Mason will miss a minimum of four games.

Henderson: The Pats ruled Henderson out for the opener last Wednesday but it seems like he'll be ready to play versus the Steelers in Week 2 on Sunday. Henderson was a full participant in practice on Wednesday. Even if Henderson returns, Rhamondre Stevenson is the No. 1 option and should maintain a heavy workload. He had 23 touches for 95 total yards versus Seattle. That said, with A.J. Brown out with injury, Henderson's explosiveness will be needed more than ever on offense.

Sampson: The Browns' backup RB is expected to miss significant time, per ESPN's Jeremy Fowler, after suffering a knee injury in Week 1's loss to the Jaguars. Raheim Sanders should serve as the backup to Quinshon Judkins while Sampson is sidelined. Jaleel McLaughlin could be elevated from the practice squad as well.

Wide Receiver

  • Nico Collins, HOU (hamstring)

  • Zay Flowers, BAL (hamstring) — DNP on Wednesday

  • Ja'Kobi Lane, BAL (wrist)

  • Ladd McConkey, LAC (rib) — DNP on Wednesday

  • Brian Thomas Jr. (shoulder) — LP at practice

  • Alec Pierce, IND (hand/wrist)

  • Omar Cooper Jr., NYJ (ankle)

  • Jalen McMillan, TB (knee)

  • Jalen Coker, CAR (ankle) — LP at practice

  • Michael Pittman Jr., PIT (foot) — LP at practice

  • Jakobi Meyers, JAX (thumb) — LP at practice

Nico Collins: The star receiver suffered a hamstring injury during Wednesday's practice, putting his Week 2 status in doubt for a matchp against Cincinnati on Sunday. Collins is coming off a seven-catch, 75-yard, one-touchdown performance in Week 1.

Ravens WRs: Flowers is considered day-to-day after exiting Week 1's win over the Colts early. He racked up a 5-150-1 line before leaving, which is a great sign for managers. Monitor him throughout practice this week (he did not practice Wednesday). Lane will be out a bit longer after suffering a fractured wrist. Reports are saying he'll miss several weeks after undergoing surgery. Rashod Bateman could benefit slightly; he played the most snaps of any Ravens receiver on Sunday (78%).

McConkey: The wideout was forced to exit after a big hit in the second half of the Chargers' loss to the Cardinals on Sunday and did not return. He posted a solid 5-82-1 line prior to leaving the contest. Los Angeles' offense struggled in the first game under Mike McDaniel. Monitor McConkey's status at practice this week as his status seems up in the air, per NFL Network. He did not practice Wednesday. If he's ruled out for Week 2, Tre' Harris is the biggest beneficiary after playing 75% of snaps on Sunday.

Tight End

  • Brock Bowers, LV (knee) — DNP on Wednesday

  • Chig Okonkwo, WAS (hamstring) — DNP on Wednesday

  • Juwan Johnson. NO (illness) — DNP on Wednesday

  • George Kittle, SF (Achilles) — LP at practice

Bowers: The Raiders TE underwent a surprise procedure on his knee and was ruled out for Week 1's win over the Dolphins. Reports say Bowers has a shot to return in Week 2 versus the Chargers, so we're going to be closely monitoring him throughout practice this week (he missed practice Wednesday). Head coach Klint Kubiak called Bowers day-to-day on Monday. Backup TE Michael Mayer had six catches on seven targets for 32 yards in the opener. If Bowers remains out, Mayer will maintain streaming value as a good floor play.

Other Injuries to Note

  • Ricky Pearsall, SF (knee) — Out for season

  • Jayden Higgins, HOU (knee) — Out for season

  • A.J. Brown, NE (ankle) — Injured reserve, could miss six weeks

  • Zach Charbonnet, SEA (knee) — PUP list

  • Josh Jacobs, GB (CEL) — Out

  • De'Zhaun Stribling, SF (ankle) — Out at least 10 weeks

  • Isiah Pacheco, DET (back) — Injured reserve, out "significant amount of time"

  • Jake Tonges, SF (ACL) — Out for season

item.title: Ashton Jeanty can carry the load
item.description: Running back touched ball more than half of Las Vegas’ offensive plays
item.content:encoded:
New Las Vegas Raiders’ head coach Klint Kubiak indicated before the start of the season that second-year starting running back Ashton Jeanty would have a heavy work load this season.

Kubiak wasn’t kidding and he didn’t waste any time showing his plans for Jeanty. The No. 6 overall pick from the 2025 draft touched the ball 29 times (23 carries and six catches). The Raiders had 68 offensive plays.

Jeanty had 102 yards rushing and added 45 yards receiving for a total of 147 yards. The Raiders had a total of 290 yards of offense. According to NFL Researcher, Jeanty had 50.7 percent of his team’s scrimmage yards in Week 1. It was the second highest rate in the league.

I wouldn’t be surprised if that high percentage rate continues.

item.title: Week 2 NFL picks against the spread, predictions for every game: Cowboys try to rebound vs. Commanders
item.description: The Cowboys defense was terrible in the season opener.
item.content:encoded:
If you didn't know it, you'd have never thought the Dallas Cowboys defense made a single change over the offseason.

Dallas looked as bad as ever on defense in the opener. The communication issues that plagued them last season hadn't gone away. They were pushed around by the New York Giants. The Cowboys got a new coordinator and five new starters (not counting linebacker DeMarvion Overshown returning from injury), and somehow nothing looked different. The Cowboys gave up the most points in franchise history last season. In Week 1, the Giants had the highest EPA (expected points added) per play in the entire NFL against Dallas' defense. Perhaps it was wrong to trust a rookie coordinator to be a magic cure and some good but not great players to completely fix the defense.

All offseason, the Cowboys were one of the most hyped teams. They spoke willingly about winning a Super Bowl even though they were 7-9-1 last season. Plenty of people who’ve grown tired of the attention the Cowboys get warned of falling for the same offseason buzz with Dallas. It's not like it has worked out for the past 30 years. And based on one game, maybe those critics were right.

The Cowboys come into Week 2 not talking about a Super Bowl anymore, but needing a win over the Washington Commanders and to avoid another embarrassing performance on defense. The defensive part shouldn't be too much to ask, but after last week it isn't a given.

Week 1 can provide some weird results. Some things we saw last week won't make any sense in a couple months. Maybe the Cowboys' performance, especially on defense, is one of those outliers. For this week we'll give the Cowboys another chance, against a Washington team that wasn't exactly smooth in its opener even though it nearly beat the Eagles. Cowboys -4 is the pick. And if Dallas plays as poorly as it did in New York, all of that offseason hype will look even sillier.

Here are the against the spread picks for the rest of the Week 2 games in the NFL:

Lions (+5.5) over Bills

Week 2 is interesting. We have to weigh what we saw in the opening week vs. what we know about these teams and thought of them over a long offseason. In Week 1, we saw Josh Allen look like Superman against a Texans defense that will be just fine, while the Lions had to successfully defend a two-point conversion to hang on to beat the Saints in overtime. The Bills are a good team, but so are the Lions. A letdown after going up 21-0 against New Orleans isn't ideal, but it happens. This will be a fun game, and a close one.

Buccaneers (-8.5) over Browns

It's not comfortable to take the Buccaneers giving more than a touchdown. They might not be that good. But it's way harder to back the Browns as long as Deshaun Watson is their quarterback. And it's not like anything else looked good for Cleveland in Week 1.

Packers (-3.5) over Jets

You're going to hear about lookahead lines (point spreads posted before the previous week kicks off) a few times. In Week 2 it's an easy way to see overreactions to a one-game sample size. Last week the Packers were -5.5 for their game at the Jets (h/t to 4for4.com). Now it's two points shorter. The Packers out-gained the Vikings 419-239 and while the fourth quarter collapse was awful, it's not like they were outplayed. The Jets did outplay the Titans, but we might look back on that as the first sign that Tennessee is one of the NFL's worst teams. The Packers should still be the far better team here.

Panthers (-2.5) over Falcons

Tough to gauge this game because we don't know who is starting at quarterback for the Falcons. If it's Michael Penix Jr., clearly the Falcons have a better shot. If it's undrafted rookie Jack Strand, we could see another Max Brosmer story. Last year people went crazy about some preseason highlights of Brosmer with the Vikings, then the undrafted rookie played really poorly when he got a shot in the regular season. The Panthers haven't covered as a favorite since 2021, which seems impossible. This is their week to do it.

Eagles (-7) over Titans

I'd rather not take a road favorite this big early in the season. And there is going to be overreaction to Tennessee's Week 1 performance that I'd normally avoid. But it was troubling how bad the Titans were in the opener. Their offense was hideous. It's not going to be any easier against the Eagles' defense. Philadelphia had its own offensive issues in Week 1, but how do the Titans move the ball in this one?

Texans (-2.5) over Bengals

I believe the Texans will have a top three defense this season. What we saw in Week 1 was Josh Allen announcing to the NFL world that he has reached a new level, which is scary. Houston's offense looked much improved in Week 1, which is a positive that could be something we're talking more about later on in the season. The Bengals won last week, but it's hard to live off turnovers and they needed all four they got to beat Tampa Bay. Cincinnati is still a slow-starting team and I won't overreact to the Texans losing to Allen's unbelievable outing in Week 1.

Saints (+8.5) over Ravens

Oddsmakers really like Baltimore. They were high on the Ravens before the season started, and that looked smart as Baltimore steamrolled the Colts in Week 1. I have some concerns about the health of Baltimore's receivers, after Zay Flowers hurt his hamstring and Ja'Kobi Lane fractured his wrist. Lamar Jackson needs someone to throw to. Meanwhile, the Saints offense got off to a poor start but finished well enough to believe they can at least keep the Ravens honest.

Bears (-4.5) over Vikings

Another tough pick without knowing exactly who is at quarterback for the Vikings. The guess is it's Carson Wentz after Kyler Murray's concussion. I have plenty of concerns about the Bears defense, but I know they'll score, even against Brian Flores' house of mirrors blitz concepts. I'd like to take the Vikings to fade some of the Bears hype, but can't depend on Wentz to outscore Chicago's offense.

Patriots (-5.5) over Steelers

The Steelers won and there still should be significant concerns about them. Their EPA on offense was 30th in the NFL and the success rate was 32nd, and that was at home against a mediocre Falcons defense. Their defensive numbers looked OK, but that was against Cooper Rush. I was not impressed with the Steelers. The Patriots lost and the week has been spent bashing Drake Maye, but an easier opponent, a home game and some extra rest will do New England well.

Chargers (-6.5) over Raiders

The lookahead line last week was Chargers -9.5. They looked awful losing to the Cardinals. But do we make much of the Raiders beating a Dolphins team that barely has an NFL roster? I don't buy that the Chargers are a terrible team all of a sudden. They just had a terrible game, which we've seen happen in Week 1 before. And the Chargers need to win with a brutal stretch of the schedule coming up.

Broncos (-2.5) over Jaguars

A true test of not overreacting to Week 1. The Jaguars looked great. The Broncos couldn't have looked worse, with the offense flailing around and the defense forgetting how to tackle. This is a blind pick that the Broncos are much better than we saw last week and also their home-field advantage in September. The Broncos are 85-34-2 at home all-time in September. It's not easy to play at high altitude early in the season.

Dolphins (+13.5) over 49ers

It's not going to be fun to back the Dolphins this season. The line of Raiders -3.5 last week was way, way too low. We haven't fully realized how bad Miami might be this season. Still, the 49ers could have a letdown after beating the Rams, and the fatigue from a long Australia trip could be real. It's just hard to trust the Dolphins to keep it close.

Seahawks (-4) over Cardinals

Seattle was -10 on the lookahead line. When Yahoo Sports' Ben Fawkes polled oddsmakers, they had the difference between Sam Darnold and Drew Lock at about 4.5 points. So the line has moved 1.5 points because the Cardinals played well against the Chargers? Seattle has a lot of extra rest, which helps not just to recover but to get Lock ready. The Seattle defense is still just fine, too.

Colts (+6.5) over Chiefs

This is a tough game to call. The Chiefs got an easy win over the Broncos. The defense looked good and Kenneth Walker III was outstanding. The passing game still remains an issue. Meanwhile, nothing looked good for the Colts in Week 1. That makes it hard to back them in Week 2 at Arrowhead Stadium. But ugly dogs cover all the time in the NFL.

Giants (+7) over Rams

We shouldn't buy into overreaction. The Rams were -9.5 on the lookahead line. Myles Garrett is great but probably not worth 2.5 points on the line. It seems like this is a good spot to take the Rams and their extra days off since the opener. But we all know that wasn't a normal opener. The Rams supposedly had an aggressive travel plan for Week 1 to avoid the Australia trip taking a toll for weeks after. But what if that's unavoidable? The NFL did neither team any favors shipping them halfway across the world for the season opener and it could linter for them both for a while. Also, the Rams looked terrible in Week 1 and while it's logical to dismiss that due to the long trip, what if it's not? At very least, we need to see the Rams look like the Rams team that was hyped up all offseason before laying a touchdown with them against a Giants team that looked pretty good in the opener. It's amazing what upgrading from Brian Daboll to John Harbaugh can do for a team.

Last week: 7-9

item.title: 49ers’ RB Christian McCaffrey can surpass a Jerry Rice milestone Sunday
item.description: 49ers running back Christian McCaffrey can also surpass Marshall Faulk in the record books
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco 49ers running back Christian McCaffrey is well on his way to being fitted for a gold jacket. He can inch one step closer as early as this Sunday by surpassing a pair of all-time greats in the record books.

McCaffrey has 98 scrimmage touchdowns (62 rushing, 36 receiving) in 113 career games. This Sunday, against the Miami Dolphins, McCaffrey can surpass none other than Jerry Rice (115 games) as the fourth-fastest player to reach 100 scrimmage touchdowns in the Super Bowl era.

The only players to reach this mark in fewer games are a pair of Hall of Famers, LaDainian Tomlinson (89 games) and Emmitt Smith (93 games), as well as Shaun Alexander (96 games).

That’s not the only record McCaffrey can break in Week 2. Additionally, McCaffrey can surpass Marshal Faulk (36 touchdown receptions) for the most touchdown receptions by a running back in the Super Bowl era.

McCaffrey failed to reach the end zone in Week 1, but the matchup is appetizing for him against the Dolphins come Sunday. Second-year back Ashton Jeanty had two touchdown receptions through the air last week against Miami. Jeanty combined for 147 yards from scrimmage on 29 touches.

If Week 1 is any indication, McCaffrey won’t have that kind of volume, but he shouldn’t need it to score twice.

item.title: Who faces more pressure in Week 2, Sean McVay or Chris Shula?
item.description: The heat is on the Los Angeles Rams and their coaches, and more NFL news on a Thursday!
item.content:encoded:
I’d argue that the headline is a bit of a trick question because both Sean McVay and Chris Shula need to get the Los Angeles Rams and their respective units back on track after a disappointing showing against the San Francisco 49ers in Week 1. Both are under tremendous pressure.

Where was the complimentary football?

The first game of the year for the Rams didn’t start out all bad, they forced an interception and had a chance to add points before Matthew Stafford gave the ball back to the 49ers on a questionable throw.

The defense tried, but failed to keep the Rams in the game as L.A.’s offense faltered, and faltered some more as the 49ers took advantage of their opportunities far more than the Rams did.

You can blast Chris Shula, he deserves blame, but the offense wasn’t good either. The complimentary football McVay talked about so much last year wasn’t there consistently in Week 1.

The pressure in on both McVay and Shula to turn things around. However, if we are being honest, one of those coaches as a much higher chance to lose their job than the other. McVay’s job shouldn’t be in jeopardy, but the pressure is on nonetheless to get this season on track.

The Rams need to get right in Week 2, and it’s not just one side of the ball that needs to look better. Everything needs to look better against the New York Giants, or else the Rams may fall to 0-2.

If you think the negative press this week was bad, just wait for an 0-2 start. Of course, the Rams can avoid that with a win, but they need to win, and winning in the NFL, is the hardest thing to do.

Sean McVay addresses narrative that Rams didn’t play to their new CBs’ strengths (ramswire)

“After the Rams added tremendous talent to their secondary, spending $175 million on contracts for Trent McDuffie and Jaylen Watson, Los Angeles believes it has a secondary that could win championships for years to come.

However, their defensive coordinator, Chris Shula, is being doubted after such a poor performance. Not only did the 49ers strike through the air, but they were also nearly unstoppable on the ground; San Francisco put up 379 yards of total offense, including 174 rushing.

So, was the issue scheme, ability, both, or a mix in addition to other factors? Head coach Sean McVay addressed the issue with the secondary and the developing narrative that despite their corners excelling in man coverage, they were used as zone defenders in Melbourne.“

West Coast Read: Can Sean McVay Turn Rams’ Nightmare Into Expected Dream Team? (foxsports)

“Since being anointed a super team this offseason, McVay has done his best to guard against complacency, tamping down talks of the Rams engineering a perfect season and hoisting the Lombardi Trophy in February for the second time in his head coaching career in the team’s home stadium.

The Rams’ media onslaught crescendoed with an appearance on “60 Minutes” over the weekend. But after laying an egg on national television in the league’s first international game Down Under, McVay just wants to get things back to normal and win a game.“

Chris Shula will have to crank up the heat for Rams defense to survive (ramblinfan)

“That’s especially true with Myles Garrett, an organic megasource of pass-rush pressure, on injured reserve. Having Aaron Donald back would help on the interior, but there’s no way Shula can repeat his passive strategy against the Giants on Monday and expect better results.

Chris Shula needs to reimagine this Rams defense

Shanahan’s dismantling of Shula and the Rams defense was a masterclass in exacting death by a thousand papercuts. Aside from one 39-yard bomb for former LA receiver DeMarcus Robinson, no play the 49ers called gained more than 18 yards – on a Brock Purdy scramble.“

Rams’ Matthew Stafford Breaks Silence After Bad News (heavy.com)

“It’ll be a collective effort to kind of pick up where he is not there. But at the same time, we all just have to play a little bit better. Obviously, we can help on the offensive side of the ball, scoring points and doing the things that we’re supposed to do, too. Football is a great team game. This will be an opportunity for us to prove that for a few weeks now, as he’s recovering.”

There are significant concerns about Garrett and his health, both over past instances and his future on the field.“

Rams’ Myles Garrett Receives Major Concern From Surgeon (sports.yahoo)

“Dr. Robert Klapper sat down with ABC7’s Curt Sandoval to speak about the concern that Garrett’s swelling is something that could be a problem.

“If you are dealing with swelling over weeks and weeks, that tells you there is more of a chronic situation going on. Is it the meniscus? Yes, but how much has the cushion- the meniscus acted like sandpaper to irritate the cartilage in addition?” Dr. Klapper said.

Garrett will undergo surgery, but that could potentially not be enough to fully heal the issues or irritation that Dr. Klapper is speaking about.“

Los Angeles Rams vs. New York Giants: How to watch, listen to and live stream Monday Night Football Week 2 (ramswire)

“The Rams and Giants last met in Week 17 of the 2023 season on New Year’s Eve where the Rams won 26-25 at MetLife Stadium in East Rutherford, N.J. Rams quarterback Matthew Stafford threw for 317 yards and one touchdown, with two interceptions. Wide receiver Puka Nacua had a team-leading 118 receiving yards on five receptions. Running back Kyren Williams had 87 rushing yards and three rushing touchdowns. Defensively, defensive end Kobie Turner had five total tackles, including two for loss, and 2.5 sacks. Defensive end Aaron Donald also had five total tackles and two for loss, adding two sacks. Outside linebacker Byron Young had four total tackles, including two for loss, and one sack.

Kickoff for Monday night’s game at SoFi Stadium is scheduled for 5:15 p.m. pacific time on ESPN and ABC.“

MERCH PHOTOS: Rams x Elwood – Commemorating the 75th anniversary of the 1951 World Championship (rams.com)

“The LA Rams x Elwood Limited Collection commemorates the 75th anniversary of the 1951 World Championship through a timeless, six-piece collection. This collaboration pays homage to championship eras of the past through Elwood’s signature approach to vintage garments, paired with the iconic logos of the 1951 LA Rams.

Available Friday, September 18 at RamsFanshop.com and in-person at the Equipment Room at SoFi Stadium.“

NFL Week 2 uniforms: Rams debut ‘Classic Sol,’ Ravens go all-white (espn.com)

“Los Angeles will wear its “Classic Sol” alternate threads against the New York Giants on “Monday Night Football.” The uniform honors the Rams’ championship in 1951, with this season marking the 75th anniversary. A sol-colored jersey includes royal blue stitched and colored numbers. The three-stripe royal blue sleeve design is a direct nod to the uniforms worn in the 1951 season. The Giants will counter by going all-white.“

NFL QB rankings, Week 2: Caleb Williams, Lamar Jackson and Trevor Lawrence soar into top five (nfl.com)

“
I begin this QB Index with a disclaimer: With only one week’s worth of evidence, there is more volatility than usual.

Reputation matters, but so do recent results. We’re a long way from solidifying the standing of many of these quarterbacks, and because we saw some unexpected outcomes in Week 1, prepare yourself for some aggressive swings.

It’ll even out eventually. For now, I have one bit of advice: Buckle up.

NOTE: Up/down arrows illustrate movement from the Week 1 QB Index.“

Giants Brace for Sean McVay’s Rams After Cowboys Upset (athlonsports)

item.title: The Honolulu Blueprint: 4 predictions for a Lions victory over the Bills
item.description: Predicting what the Detroit Lions will do to earn a victory over the Buffalo Bills in Week 2 of the 2026 season.
item.content:encoded:
The Detroit Lions and Buffalo Bills kick off Week 2 with a Thursday night matchup at the Bills’ new home, Highmark Stadium. Both teams won their opening games on their offense’s final possession and will look to start their season with a coveted 2-0 record.

“These guys are obviously a really good opponent,” Lions coach Dan Campbell said at his Monday press conference. “It’s opening night, out at their place Thursday night. It’ll be electric. It’s going to be a great atmosphere. We’ll be looking forward to that; excellent opponent. This will be a big-time game here early in the year.”

Let’s take a closer look at this matchup and predict what the Lions will do to earn a victory over the Bills in this week’s Honolulu Blueprint.

This week’s predictions preview is sponsored by the folks at FanDuel Sportsbook, who currently have the Lions listed at +1700 to win this year’s Super Bowl and 4.5-point underdogs in Week 2.

Bills base schemes

For a detailed look at the opposing scheme, make sure you check out our complementary breakdown piece: Lions Week 2 preview: Breaking down the Bills’ offensive and defensive schemes.

Prediction 1: Lots of Gibbs runs out of 11 personnel

One question the Lions had entering this season was whether they could improve their rushing efficiency. In Week 1, things looked much better, as Jahmyr Gibbs finished with 156 rushing yards (5.4 yards per carry) and a rushing success rate of 58.62% (fifth-highest in the NFL, per Sumer Sports).

Where things get interesting is when you look at the efficiency rate in different personnel settings, specifically 11 personnel (1 running back, 1 tight end, 3 wide receivers). In this popular personnel group, Gibbs ran the ball 13 times for 107 yards, and a success rate of 76.9%, best in the NFL amongst RBs with at least three carries in this grouping.

What was notable against the Saints was that they often matched personnel grouping by countering 11 with their nickel formation and presenting a lighter box to rush against. This matters because the Bills do the same thing, and at an even more dramatic rate.

Last week, when the Bills consistently matched the Texans’ 11 personnel with nickel, Houston’s backs saw success. Woody Marks ran the ball five times for 33 yards with a 60% success rate (sixth), while David Montgomery ran for 15 yards on four carries with a 50% success rate (12th). Both marks bested the team’s overall success rate for the game (46.9%).

Based on the Lions’ and Texans’ Week 1 success, it’s in Detroit’s best interest to keep the Bills in nickel as much as possible. Especially when you factor in Amon-Ra St. Brown…

Prediction 2: Another heavy dose of Amon-Ra St. Brown

The Bills defense has gone through significant change this offseason, switching from a 4-2 to a 3-4, and it’s going to take time to acclimate to the new scheme, which should play to the Lions’ advantage. Last week, Buffalo played match defense, deploying base personnel around 40% of the time, then splitting their 60% sub-package work between nickel (36%) and dime (24%) formations.

After losing Taron Johnson in free agency, the Bills signed Dee Alford to man the slot, and he should draw a lot of matchups against Amon-Ra St. Brown. Here’s an excerpt from NFLPro (NextGen) on Alford:

Dee Alford took over the slot for Buffalo in Week 1, playing 86.0% of snaps from slot, the role Taron Johnson held in 2025. Alford was targeted on 21.8% of his coverage snaps last season, the highest rate among cornerbacks (min. 300 coverage snaps) and allowed 1.5 yards per coverage snap (10th-most).

In Week 1, Alford allowed only two receptions for 23 yards on four targets, but the Bills defense as a whole struggled when in nickel, allowing an EPA of 0.14 (26th best in the NFL) and a success rate of 53.8% (28th).

St. Brown is coming off a Week 1 performance in which he caught 10 of his 14 targets and found the end zone twice, but even that wasn’t as impressive as his 12-catch, 193-yard, touchdown performance the last time he played the Bills.

“It’s the consistency of what he does, the details,” Campbell said of his All-Pro wide receiver. “And more importantly, he’s a pit bull. The ball’s in the air; it’s his ball. And there’s a competitiveness and a willpower that comes with that, and he’s going to make that play.”

Prediction 3: Lions blitz to offset Bills’ aggressive offense

“Ultimately, I don’t care what they throw at us; the quarterback is the key to all of this. And if we don’t make him go the long hard way every time, it can get very difficult.” — Dan Campbell on Bills QB Josh Allen.

Josh Allen can do it all. He can throw to every level of the field, is comfortable in the pocket, understands the offensive system, and is a threat to pull the ball and run at any time. In Week 1 against the Texans’ elite defense, he completed 20-of-29 passing attempts for 334 yards and two passing touchdowns, for a 130.5 passer rating. He also ran the ball six times for 23 yards and two more touchdowns.

The Lions will need to find ways to disrupt Allen’s tempo and aggressiveness to slow the Bills offense. Lions defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard has made an effort to disguise their intentions on defense this year, and he’ll need to be sharp and creative against Allen. One of the crafty ways he’ll likely try to confuse Allen is by blitzing his defensive backs.

Roger McCreary had a solid Week 1, generating four pressures (all under 2.5 seconds per NFL Pro), but the Lions will return their preferred nickel starter in Week 2: Christian Izien. The Lions quickly signed Izien in free agency and immediately inserted him into the starting lineup because of his aggressive nature. While Izien is returning from injury, he was very close to playing in Week 1, and it appeared the Lions elected not to push him into game action because they wanted him 100% ready for this specific game.

Look for Izien to be a key defensive catalyst in disrupting Allen.

Prediction 4: Lions take advantage of turnover opportunities

“If a mistake is made, we have to capitalize. We have to. We have to make that play.” — Campbell earlier in the week.

While Campbell didn’t specifically reference the Bills’ three potential turnovers on the final drive (!) of Week 1, I got the impression that is what he was referencing when he made the above statement.

Down one point with about six-and-a-half minutes remaining in regulation, Allen fumbled on the first play of the drive, but Buffalo recovered and maintained possession. Eight plays later, Texans corner Derek Stingley punched the ball away from Bills running back James Cook, but again, the Bills were able to recover. Five plays later, Allen threw a deep pass into the end zone, right into the hands of Texans corner Kamari Lassiter, but he couldn’t secure the interception as he awkwardly adjusted to the ball and fell to the ground. The next play, Allen hit Bills wide receiver Joshua Palmer for a 34-yard touchdown that became the winning score.

If the Texans capitalize on any of those three turnover-worthy plays, they would’ve had a real chance to put the game away and secure a victory.

The Lions capitalized on three turnover opportunities in Week 1, as DJ Wonnum recovered a punch-out fumble from Roger McCreary, while Chuck Clark and Derrick Barnes each made an interception. Turnovers tend to come in bunches, and they’ll need to stay opportunistic in this game.

item.title: Broncos vs. Jaguars: 3 Things to Watch for in Week 2
item.description: Here are three storylines I’ll be watching closely on Sunday when the Denver Broncos host the Jacksonville Jaguars.
item.content:encoded:
The Denver Broncos follow up their Week 1 loss to the Kansas City Chiefs by hosting the Jacksonville Jaguars on Sunday. The Jaguars were just one of three teams to deliver the Broncos a defeat last season. In a way, this matchup has the allure of a revenge game. Most importantly, the opportunity to get back on track and avoid going 0-2 to start off the 2026 season. Here are three storylines I’m going to keep a close eye on throughout the game.

Will the Broncos show signs of life on offense?

I figured there would always be a little bit of a learning curve for Offensive Coordinator Davis Webb and the Broncos’ offense this season. That happens with change. However, I didn’t expect them to be as flat as they were on Monday Night Football versus the Chiefs.

There was no dedication to the run. Their passing attack was a joke. It’s almost impossible to win a football game when both phases on offense look that bad.

In last year’s defeat to the Jaguars, Bo Nix had to throw 47 times. That’s a recipe for failure and can’t happen if Denver wants to win on Sunday. The Broncos went just 5-of-14 on third down and were 1-of-3 on fourth down conversions in that matchup, on top of turning the ball over twice.

They need to establish the run. Feed J.K. Dobbins, RJ Harvey, and give Jonah Coleman an opportunity to shine. Nix and the wide receivers need to be on the same page. Jacksonville’s defense is quite opportunistic and winning the turnover battle will be an absolute must to get to 1-1 on the season.

Can the defense embark on a drastic turnaround on a short week?

The defense gave up numerous big plays that resulted in touchdowns for the Chiefs. Kenneth Walker II had one of the best games of his career and the defense looked like they completely had forgotten how to tackle. It was certainly embarrassing to watch, but not as bad as the 70-point shellacking the Miami Dolphins gave Defensive Coordinator Vance Joseph and his players in 2023.

Last December, the Jaguars put up 34 points on the scoreboard—the most of any opponent in ’25. That loss, just like the Chiefs, was humbling for Denver. Jacksonville converted over 50-percent of their third downs and had several long touchdown drives. Whether it was on the ground or through the air, Liam Coen’s gameplan against the Broncos’ defense in key situations was virtually flawless.

On a short week, Joseph and the defense don’t have a lot of time to fix things. Going up against Trevor Lawrence, who is playing some of the best football of his career, poses a significant challenge for them. They will have to be at their best to limit his top-tier playmaking ability.

Great teams rebound and respond to adversity: Will Denver do that?

One game isn’t indicative of how the remaining sixteen will play out. That being said, I’m concerned about what’s to come and the team’s potential this season after their disastrous showing at Arrowhead on MNF.

The Broncos won fourteen games last year. And in some ways, I think they may have overachieved. Your mileage may vary. All things considered, I certainly didn’t expect them to win that much in ‘26. They’ve got a first-place schedule and a lot of teams got better over the course of the offseason.

Regression, in some fashion, happens quite often in the NFL. The Jaguars will be a formidable foe for Denver. In the weeks to come, the Broncos will go up against a bunch of quality teams. Sure, the Broncos have started off slow in Head Coach Sean Payton’s time with the team, but this certainly isn’t the time to do that.

To be the best, you have to beat the best. To be a Super Bowl competitor, you have to win against good teams. And that’s what the Jaguars are—a really good football team. Will Denver rise to the occasion and get back to a .500 ball club or will they fall into a two-game hole to start the season. We will find out on Sunday.

item.title: Saints Rookie Report: Week 2 preview
item.description: A overall tough first game for the rookies, and it may be the same in Week 2
item.content:encoded:
The New Orleans Saints had a very up-and-down first game of the season, but I think what surprised me most was the lack of impact from the rookies. Maybe I was a bit too confident in the Saints’ use of these players, but it was an overall quiet day from the first-year players, aside from maybe two who stood out.

Week 2 may be different, and if the Saints want to win, it should be.

DT Christen Miller

On the Saints roster, Christen Miller had to overcome both Davon Godchaux and Nathen Shepherd in front of him, but he still got on the field against the Lions. Godchaux didn’t have a great game, and Shepherd made some plays here and there, but I saw no reason Miller wouldn’t be on the field. He did have a hold in the game, which was the main knock, but overall, he looked strong and performed well enough to consider playing him more.

Against the Baltimore Ravens, Miller’s strenght and run defense are a necessity. RB Derrick Henry is inevitable. Stopping him is one of the most difficult things to do in the NFL, and it doesn’t help that Lamar Jackson is back there with the threat of running himself. Miller must see the field more.

TE Oscar Delp

Delp didn’t play in Week 1 because of his hamstring injury, and it looked like the Saints missed him. Juwan Johnson and Noah Fant both made plays in the air, but Delp’s blocking would have helped a lot. There were a couple of plays where Johnson’s blocking could have been better (although it wasn’t bad blocking), and moments where Treyton Welch did struggle holding blocks. Of course, we haven’t had consistency from Delp in the air, but I do think his presence would have changed the game a bit.

Now for the Ravens matchup, I’m not sure Delp plays. Hamstrings are tricky, and the group of three that played against the Lions were not bad, just could have been better.

OG Jeremiah Wright

Wright also didn’t play in Week 1, but it was because Cesar Ruiz started in front of him. This will be a bit more about Ruiz and why a change could be made. Nothing on Sunday showed us that the improvements Mickey Loomis noted at the end of last season happened. Ruiz struggled in run blocking, was pushed back multiple times in pass protection, and was just flat-out beat throughout the game. To give Ruiz a compliment, he was a bit more consistent as a pass protector, just not where the Saints want him to be.

I doubt a change will be made anytime soon; I just wanted to note that with Wright having a great end to the preseason, the Saints may want to see what they have in the rookie.

WRs Bryce Lance

Although Lance wasn’t listed as WR3 entering this game, he played like it, and the Saints put him in that role early in the matchup. They must have seen something to know Lance would be the better fit against this Lions defense, and it worked. Lance got open in the short game, had some nice run-after-the-catch moments, blocked well, and made one of the day’s biggest plays, converting a massive fourth-and-long.

It’s going to be a more difficult matchup against the Ravens, but Lance may be the perfect WR3 option to make the tough catches when needed, similar to Devaughn Vele

WR Barion Brown

Barion Brown’s inclusion in the offense was probably the surprise of the day. The rookie, after a really impressive preseason, did not play much. He had one handoff that went for a short gain, but that was about it. I do wonder if the Lions just really played him well and Lance was just the better fit for this matchup. The questionable moments happened on the kick returns, which were not great.

The Ravens’ secondary is very good, and with head coach Jesse Minter being defensively focused, I think this could be another quiet game from Brown.

OT Mason Murphy

Murphy was a healthy scratch against the Lions, and that should be the case again in Week 2.

Injured players:

  • WR Jordyn Tyson
  • DB Lorenzo Styles Jr.

item.title: Steelers film room: Pittsburgh trends on offense, defense against the Falcons
item.description: Before we flip the page to the Steelers’ next opponents — our preview of the New England Patriots matchup is out Friday — we here at Read & React wanted to take one last look at the film from Week 1, and take stock of any interesting trends or tidbits we felt worth sharing. We […]
item.content:encoded:
Before we flip the page to the Steelers’ next opponents — our preview of the New England Patriots matchup is out Friday — we here at Read & React wanted to take one last look at the film from Week 1, and take stock of any interesting trends or tidbits we felt worth sharing. We haven’t decided if we’ll do a film room each week in-season, or toggle between that and doing what we have in the past in discussing the trending Steelers narratives in the media at large.

At least for this week, we’ve opted for the former, as we couldn’t bring ourselves to add another article with hand-wringing about the Joey Porter Jr. contract situation, attempts to interpret the various Aaron Rodgers and Mike McCarthey soundbites throughout the week, nor give any in-depth takes on former coach Mike Tomlin as an in-studio analyst — though I think he had more ups than downs, and I hope NBC doesn’t try to over-sanitize his personality; we don’t need more Jason Garrett types!

So with that in mind, let’s dive into the tape with what Ryland and Ryan found noteworthy about Week 1’s performance.

Defense

RB: So much was made about how creative and at times complicated Patrick Graham’s Steelers defense would be in 2026, but to start off the season, Pittsburgh’s new coordinator kept things fairly simple.

There were some twists rushing the passer, a healthy dose of coverage rotations, and some of Graham’s signature creepers at the line of scrimmage. But overall, Pittsburgh’s game plan was fairly straightforward by NFL standards.

Pittsburgh blitzed at a league-low 7.7%, primarily relying on a four-man rush. According to Next Gen Stats, the Steelers played zone coverage exclusively when the Falcons dropped back to pass — though it should be noted, as Graham did in a later press conference, that some of those reps used match concepts, which have similarities to man coverage. And while some off-ball linebacker snaps for Nick Herbig were a new wrinkle in the Steelers’ three-outside linebacker package, there wasn’t much in the realm of exotic formations or schematics.

Why were things so simple? My guess would be that the Steelers rightfully recognized their defense is clearly more talented than the Cooper Rush-led Falcons offense, and saw no need to complicate things. Despite Pittsburgh rarely blitzing, the Steelers managed a 15.4% sack rate, the league’s second-best mark in Week 1.

Elite running back Bijan Robinson was a problem, as expected, with 90 receiving yards and plenty of missed tackles in the process. Despite this, he was held to a manageable four yards per carry in the run game. And Atlanta’s next-leading receiver, the talented Drake London, was held to 29 yards as Rush completed just 12/22 passes for 143 yards.

Altogether, a lack of uber-confusing concepts likely helped the defensive players simply line up and make plays. Keeping things simple can be a detriment when a team lacks enough talent, but we’ve also seen plenty of elite defenses, like last year’s Texans or the Legion of Boom-era Seahawks, suffocate opposing offenses when the right collection of players can master a straightforward scheme.

For the Steelers on Sunday, that resulted in arguably the best game of inside linebacker Payton Wilson’s career.

For much of the summer, I projected my hope that a Year 3 breakout from the talented Wilson would be possible under Graham’s guidance. That campaign got off to a good start in Week 1. I’m not sure if I’ve ever seen Wilson look so fast and confident on the football field. He logged 13 total tackles, including two for loss, and looked both quick and decisive in coverage. And while he’s still not a thumper defending the run, the game looks like it has slowed down for him, with Wilson seeing success knifing through blocks near the line of scrimmage to make plays.

Wilson’s play, as well as high-end performances from T.J. Watt, Cam Heyward and Alex Highsmith, were probably the biggest individual storylines for the Steelers defense.

However, I was also impressed by the contributions of some newcomers on the defense.

Both safety Jaquan Brisker and cornerback Jamel Dean were solid in coverage (Brisker recorded a nice interception on an overthrow in zone; Dean got run by when flat-footed on one play but otherwise looked fine), but both made their biggest impacts as tacklers.

Dean looked like a heat-seeking missile at times and managed to force a fumble on Robinson.

Brisker was fearless when filling holes in the run game. Even if he didn’t always make a clean tackle, he clearly affected a number of plays.

One of the hits on Robinson was a true bone-crusher, too.

View Link

Besides taking advantage of misfires and poor reads from Rush, Graham’s zone-heavy scheme (with a heavy dose of cover 4) allowed the team’s aggressive defensive backs to keep the game in front of them and crash down when needed.

A more underrated contributor was new defensive lineman Sebastian Joseph-Day, who logged just 18 snaps in a rotational role but still managed to stand out on several reps. His power is a real asset, and having a player of his caliber outside the main starting lineup speaks to the team’s overall depth at the position.

We’ll end with the Steelers’ biggest name on defense, T.J. Watt, who looked like his prime self once again against Atlanta with two sacks, a pick-six and another tackle for loss. Attentive watchers would’ve noticed Watt saw a number of rushes from the right side of the defense — he’s been almost exclusively a left-side rusher for much of his career — showing some of the “Watt moving around the formation” hype could finally be coming true under the defense’s new coordinator.

Did Watt look especially different coming from the right side? Did defenses look unusually perplexed? Not exactly, but his first rep from the blind side resulted in a sack, which means the idea resulted in some success. It’s also a good sign for the Steelers continuing to matchup hunt and mix and match the team’s arsenal of pass rushers down the road.

View Link

What’s exciting about Graham as the defensive coordinator is that it’s difficult to know what he’ll bring to the table next week. He’s made a career of being adaptable to the players he has and the opponents he faces, something he made clear to the media in Tuesday’s press conference.

“My philosophy is what’s best for that week, usually … what we think is best to beat the opponent and make sure our guys are able to play fast,” Graham said when asked about the team’s zone-heaviness in Week 1.

Graham had a similar response when asked about the lack of blitzing. “I mean, I’m going to tell you, we’re going to try to do what’s best for the game that week,” he said. One game we might have ‘blitz zero’ 20 times in a game. The next week might not blitz one time. We might ‘drop eight’ 20 times. I can’t tell you.”

“If it’s physical, if we’re running around, attacking the ball, I think everybody in this town would appreciate that because that’s Steeler football, in my opinion — part of the identity of Steeler football, defensive football. … How we play, more than what we do, is important to me,” he continued.

That philosophy was clear in Sunday’s win. Much tougher offenses await later in the season, but it was as good a start as could be expected for the Patrick Graham era of Steelers defense.

Offense

RP: While Ryland’s given us plenty of reasons to be intrigued by the defense, unfortunately the Pittsburgh offense is here to pour some cold water on the proceedings. That isn’t to say there can’t be improvement as the season progresses. It’s only been one week, after all, and the Steelers are both learning a new system and trying to shake off the offseason rust. But the Steelers can’t continue to play offense like they did on Sunday and expect to win many games. Pittsburgh converted just three of its third-down attempts into first downs, and failed two fourth-down attempts, though one was a botched operation on a field goal, not a genuine attempt to go for it.

While there will be time to discuss the passing game in further detail in the future, the topic of Pittsburgh’s passing difficulties has already been discussed on BTSC, and it’s clear the Steelers had some bad luck with some pass interference — including both some questionable OPI calls and some missed DPI calls — and also left plenty of meat on the bone with inopportune drops and failures to win contested catches. McCarthy also took a lot of the blame upon himself for calling a “herky-jerky game” and failing to get any of the Steelers’ playmakers in a rhythm.

The passing game was certainly frustrating, but what gave me the most concern was the rushing game.

Excluding kneel-downs at the end of the game, the Steelers ran the ball 18 times for just 61 yards. Jaylen Warren had a decent day and looked like one of the Steelers’ more explosive playmakers on offense, but he also had a fumble and had just as many runs gain less than four yards (5) as he did runs that exceeded that mark. Rico Dowdle had an especially tough go of things. After picking up six yards on his first carry, he had just one carry that exceeded three yards the rest of the day.

I wanted to diagnose what the root of Pittsburgh’s issues were and see if there were any schematic or personnel patterns that might explain why the sledding was so tough for the Steelers’ ground game. What I found was that it didn’t really matter whether the Steelers had 11 personnel or multiple tight ends on the field. They were out of sync regardless, though they were particularly bad running out of shotgun.

Some other tidbits I found:

  • Of the Steelers’ 18 rushing attempts, 11 came on first down. All other attempts, excluding kneel-downs, were attempted on second down. The Steelers threw the ball on 16 first-down plays.
  • The Steelers attempted 42 passes and just 18 rushing attempts.
  • Steelers runs to the left (9 attempts): 3.1 YPC (Warren 3.5 YPC, Dowdle 2.3 YPC)
  • Steelers runs to the right (5 attempts): 3.2 YPC (Warren 7.0 YPC, Dowdle 0.6 YPC)
  • Steelers runs up the middle (4 attempts): 4.3 YPC (Warren 5.5 YPC, Dowdle 3.0 YPC)
  • Steelers in 11P: With Washington at tight end (6 attempts, 3.0 YPC); With Freiermuth at tight end (2 attempts, 0.0 YPC)
  • Warren’s stat line was buoyed by three late runs (an 8-yarder, 17-yarder, and 9-yarder) that totaled 34 yards (74% of his output)

Even before throwing on the tape, it’s easy to see why McCarthy was critical of himself. Offenses he’s called, especially with Rodgers at quarterback, have always skewed pass-heavy, but the imbalance of run-versus-pass in this game was stark. It also didn’t set the offense up for easy third-down attempts. If we include the two third-down plays that were wiped out due to pass interference — one on the offense and one on the defense — the Steelers’ average distance to go on third down was 7.7 yards.

McCarthy also could have called more play-action, considering how well it worked for the Steelers. Even with the inconsistencies running the ball, Rodgers completed 6-of-8 play-action pass attempts for 65. The two incomplete passes were both instances where the Steelers left points on the board. One was a pass to Metcalf in the end zone, where the defensive back did grab his arm before the ball arrived, but Metcalf still managed to get both hands on the ball. The second was on a bootleg to the left, where Rodgers missed Jaylen Warren wide on a pass the running back would have walked in for six with a better ball.

Now you might be saying to yourself, “But Ryan, you said you weren’t going to be talking about the passing game. Yet here you are talking about play action.”

To which I say, touché. I guess I was running some play fakes of my own just now. But more importantly, I think it’s an interesting part of understanding how this offense could work together better in the weeks ahead, that is, if the Steelers can iron out some of the kinks. As you’ll see in some of the following plays, the Steelers run game wasn’t scaring the Falcons defense much, but the Steelers were still efficient with play action despite that. Imagine how dangerous that could be if the Steelers develop a threatening run game.

So what went wrong? I don’t think it’s as simple as blaming this on any one player. To have a functioning and effective running attack, the offensive line, tight ends, fullbacks, and even the wide receivers need to work in sync as blockers. The ball carrier must also make the right reads and hit the holes provided to them with the proper timing and intensity. Often, it only takes one weak link to doom a designed run. I thought the Steelers’ struggles in this game, more often than not, fell on the blockers rather than the backs, though Warren and Dowdle can certainly stand to improve on this game.

In particular, I thought left tackle Troy Fautanu and right guard Spencer Anderson had some difficult reps as run blockers in this game.

While there were some decent reps from Fautanu on other plays, his issues with leverage on Sunday jumped out to me in a game where the Steelers attempted disproportionately fewer rushing attempts. I watched Fautanu a lot on film last year, and there are games where he kicks butt as a run blocker. He’s not a player who lacks the necessary power to move defenders. But when he does have struggles, it’s on reps where his technique gets sloppy, and he loses his leverage.

Sunday was just one of those games for Fautanu. In the clip above, he doesn’t even do anything egregiously wrong. I think you could ask him to move his defender off his spot with a little more power, but Fautanu wins his rep if not for Warren tripping on the offensive tackle’s leg. If Warren is able to keep his feet, plant, and accelerate out of that cut, all he needs to do is make the linebacker (53) miss, and the Steelers have a positive gain instead of a stop at the line of scrimmage.

It certainly wasn’t Fautanu’s best performance, but Anderson was the player that left me with the most concern. Coming out of college, the knock on Anderson’s draft profile was a lack of pop to his blocks, and a tendency to find himself leaning and off balance. All of those flaws were on display against Atlanta, though as you’ll see in these clips, he isn’t the only one losing on some of these reps.

Overall, the unit just rarely looked fully in sync.

As for the running backs, I think we all are familiar with Warren and his skill set. He remains the team’s best running back, both with the ball in his hands and as a pass blocker. That said, I’m not ready to throw in the towel on Dowdle as the RB2 just yet. While I don’t think Dowdle has the same burst and decisiveness as Warren, I lean toward the line’s performance as the biggest factor in his poor Week 1 stat line. Of course, that doesn’t mean I don’t think there are plays he needs to execute better, like in the following clip.

Still, even with this showing against the Falcons, I do think this is a team that can get better. While I don’t think Dylan Cook particularly contributed to the team’s running woes, I do think getting Iheanachor into the lineup would be a net positive for this unit. He has obvious power and plus-mobility that we got glimpses of in the preseason.

Beyond that, I’d keep an eye on Anderson. He’s a cool story as a former seventh-round pick who’s climbed to a starting position, but he needs to show some improvement if he wants to keep the job. The Steelers have plenty of options should his struggles continue. They could always kick Dylan Cook inside if they believe he is still one of their best five linemen, plus they have veterans they could call on like Brock Hoffman and Ryan McCollum. I don’t believe rookie Gennings Dunker is quite ready to start, but I felt similarly about McCormick as a rookie, and he responded well to being thrown into the fire. Dunker was often compared to McCormick during the draft cycle, for what it’s worth.

Will the Steelers be able to get the run game right in Week 2 against New England? Come back Friday for our New England preview.

item.title: Panthers vs Falcons: Week 2 storylines to watch
item.description: Breaking down the key storylines going into this week’s matchup between the Carolina Panthers and Atlanta Falcons
item.content:encoded:
Hello CSR! I’m here to break down the biggest storylines to watch following an explosive but disappointing week 1 matchup against the Chicago Bears. The Panthers’ offense had its first week 1 coming out party in years, unfortunately the Bears’ party was much larger. Luckily, everyone else in the NFC South lost, including the Falcons, so this is as good a time as ever for the Panthers to right the ship and improve on the things that did them in the first game of the season.

Offense: More of that, please!

If you looked at the Panthers offense during week 1 in isolation, you’d think the unit as a whole had a pretty complete game. Sure, there’s always those stops that happen in an NFL game, but even Bryce Young’s lone interception was basically just a decision to go after points in the waning moments of the first half. The offensive line was solid, Jalen Coker and Tetairoa McMillan continued all of their momentum from 2025, and Bryce Young came out aggressive throwing the ball down the field and confident in his decision making. So while the loss was surely demoralizing, the offense cannot dwell on it and must simply come out swinging like they did against the Bears. There will be more opportunity for explosive plays down the field in the passing game, and while the Falcons did hold the Steelers to only 58 rushing cards, Jaylen Warren managed to average 4.6 yards per carry on 1o attempts against them while Aaron Rodgers wasn’t all that effective throwing the ball 40 times. The Panthers should be able to attack this defense in much the same way they attacked the Bears and see success.

Defense: Less of that, please!

Meanwhile, the Panthers defense surrendered 59 points against the Bears, while they ran for close to 300 yards against the unit and Caleb Williams absolutely balled out in the passing game. I wouldn’t expect the Falcons to have the same kind of game passing (more on that later), but Bijan Robinson could very easily give them major issues in the rushing game if this defense can’t lock in here. They need to maintain their assignments, especially on perimeter runs and QB scrambles. Princely Umanmielen, you gotta contain the QB dawg.

But the biggest thing they must eliminate is mental mistakes that cost the defense easy field position. We cannot see defensive linemen jumping offsides on key plays or hitting the quarterback on 3rd and long and causing roughing the passer penalties. In the end, no matter how you felt about the Panthers defense on Sunday, there were several key preventable penalties that cost them the most in a game that was neck and neck going into the 3rd quarter.

X Factor: Uhhh, which quarterback are they playing?

Its been a wild week if you follow along with Falcons news on social media this week. As of right now, Cooper Rush is expected to be starting. But the Falcons coaching staff refuses to reveal their hand so throughout the week there’s been talk of Michael Penix potentially stepping in and starting this week. Both quarterbacks carry with them a vastly different game plan for the defense. The unit came out looking very unprepared at times against the Bears, and that can’t happen this week no matter who the QB is.

What storylines are you watching this week, Panthers fans?

item.title: How did Jaxson Dart get a mediocre PFF grade in the Cowboys game?
item.description: It’s all about what PFF values most, which may differ from what you value
item.content:encoded:
quixotic – hopelessly impractical especially in the pursuit of ideals (Merriam-Webster)

Shortly after I joined the BBV staff as a weekly contributor in 2022, Ed asked me if I’d be willing to write the weekly post on Pro Football Focus grades after each New York Giants game. It’s a somewhat thankless task, though I find it personally educational to try to figure out why they gave a player the grade they did.

I’ve tried over the years to explain what I know about how PFF grades and how they are determined, and I’ve even published a couple of pieces specifically on that topic. Judging by the reactions to my last piece after the Dallas game, none of it has had much effect. Many of you were incensed in particular that Jaxson Dart only received a PFF passing grade of 68.5, which is in the 60-70 range of grades that PFF regards as average, or expected, play. That for a night when he went 23-of-29 (79.3%) for 230 yards, 3 TDs, and no interceptions. I’m sure that Giants fans will take a stat line like that every week of the season. PFF looked at it and said, “at the upper end of average.”

In general, you don’t want to know the details of how the sausage is made, but when you don’t like the taste of the final product, peeking behind the curtain can be a useful thing. PFF does give us some peeks behind the curtain. Generally, they emphasize that they grade process, not results. That makes sense for several reasons. Think of the two most recent unforgettable passing plays in Giants history:

In the 2008 Super Bowl, Eli Manning made perhaps the most famous pass in Super Bowl history, hitting David Tyree deep downfield, the latter making the famous “helmet catch,” which kept the game-winning drive alive and led to spoiling the Patriots’ perfect season. I don’t know how PFF graded that throw. I do know that they credited Manning with one “turnover-worthy play” (TWP) in that game; that pass might or might not have been it. Manning heroically escaped pressure on that play to get the pass off, but let’s face it, he just put it up for grabs. If not for Tyree’s superhuman effort, Rodney Harrison might have intercepted that ball and it would have been lights out for the Giants.

Four years later the Giants were in a similar situation, needing a TD to beat the Patriots in the Super Bowl. This time, it was the Manning-to-Manningham pass play that became part of history. Manning-to-Manningham had everything: Crucial situation, explosive pass play, unbelievable accuracy of ball placement in-bounds but between two defenders, plus an absolutely great catch by Manningham. We know that that pass received a grade of +2 from PFF, the highest grade it’s possible for them to give, because they used it to explain what a +2 grade is (https://www.pff.com/grades).

All well and good, but it’s all the -1, -0.5, 0, +0.5, and +1 grades that make up most of a football game. This week PFF apparently noticed that Chicago Bears fans were mildly upset, to say the least, that their QB, Caleb Williams, received a passing grade of 64.0 after his 21-for-29, 269 yards, 2 TDs, and 0 INTs performance in a 59-37 win over Carolina. Pretty similar to Dart’s stat line, and a pretty similar PFF grade.

At the heart of PFF’s grading system is an assumption that an NFL player shouldn’t get credit for the basic things he is supposed to do. If you’re a starting quarterback in the NFL you’re expected to complete easy passes. No participation trophy. If you go 20-for-20 and everything is a short pass where the receiver is wide open, they’re not impressed. It’s like not being impressed if the mailman shows up every day and actually puts the mail in the mailbox. The question they ask is: Don’t tell me about the result – how good was the process that led to that result? In the case of Williams, he dropped back 40 times, and 23 of those times he got a grade of 0. He had one terrible play for which he got a -1.5, 8 plays with a grade of +0.5, and 1 play with a grade of +1. No +1.5 or +2 plays. That’s how you wind up with an average overall grade.

But you don’t care about Caleb Williams, you care about Dart. Fortunately the article gives us a peek – but only a peek – at how they viewed what Dart did on Sunday:

Willams was only 12th-highest in positively graded plays. Trevor Lawrence and Lamar Jackson were the two highest. Sitting there at No. 3, though, is Jaxson Dart, who achieved a positive grade on 32.35% of his dropbacks.

They also show us their rankings for negatively graded plays:

Dart comes in sixth-lowest on this list. So put those two things together – third-highest in positively graded dropbacks and sixth-lowest in negatively graded dropbacks – and I think the result matches what most of you – and I – thought of Dart’s performance. Lots of good reps, not many bad reps.

If PFF stopped there, I suspect that we’d all be pretty happy with it. But they don’t stop there. Positively graded plays go from +0.5 (nice) to +2 (wow!). Negatively graded plays go from -0.5 (oops) to -2 (omigod, what were you thinking?). The two extremes are what they refer to as “big-time throws” (BTT) and “turnover-worthy plays” (TWP). Both of those may or may not show up on the stat sheet. If Dart throws a beautiful pass deep downfield and the receiver drops it, it’s 0-for-1 on the stat sheet but it’s a BTT nonetheless to PFF because Dart went above and beyond what you expect of an average QB. Likewise if he throws the ball right into the midsection of a defensive back and the defender drops it, it’s 0-for-1 on the stat sheet but a TWP nonethless to PFF, i.e., the fact that the defender was inept doesn’t absolve the QB of his terrible throw. I don’t know how they exactly do the math to come up with the final grade, but those are the factors that go into it.

They only show the detailed analysis for Williams, but they make it available for every other QB as well…for a $199.99 “PFF Pro” subscription. I don’t have that. So I’m going to try to guess at how they reacted to every Dart dropback from the film and compare it to what they actually said. The grades below are my guesses after watching the film. Remember, nothing wrong with a zero, it’s just an “as expected for an NFL QB” result.

First Quarter:

10:49: Dart to Nabers, 9 yards (grade = 0)

9:43: Dart short to Ricard, incomplete, deflected (grade = -0.5)

7:32: Dart to Likely, 13 yards (grade = 0)

0:33: Dart incomplete to Nabers, almost intercepted (grade = -1)

0:29: Dart to Likely, 7 yards (grade = 0)

Second Quarter:

14:13: Dart to Nabers, 7 yards (grade = 0)

5:01: Dart pulls it down, scrambles forward, sack but no yards lost (grade = -0.5)

4:19: Dart incomplete long to Fields, almost sacked (grade = 0)

4:14: Dart pressured, pass to Likely, 19 yards (grade = +1.5)

3:01: Dart short to Fields, 19 yards (grade = +0.5)

2:36: Dart sacked, -8 yards, fumbles, Runyan recovers (-2)

0:49: Dart to Nabers, incomplete (grade = 0)

0:45: Dart to Fields, 6 yards (grade = +0.5)

0:40: Dart to Nabers, 16 yards (grade = +0.5)

0:35: Dart to Mooney, 18 yards (grade = +1)

0:31: Dart to Likely, 5 yards (grade = 0)

0:20: Dart to Likely, 15 yards, TD (grade = +0.5)

Third quarter:

13:41: Dart to Johnson, 9 yards (grade = 0)

11:25: Dart to Nabers, 16 yards (grade = 0)

9:55: Dart to Mooney, 9 yards (grade = 0)

8:28: Dart to Nabers, 13 yards (grade = +0.5)

6:59: Dart to Likely, 2 yards, TD (grade = 0)

Fourth quarter:

12:10: Dart to Fields deep, incomplete (grade = -0.50)

11:16: Dart to Singletary, loss of 7 yards (grade = -1)

10:27: Dart to Nabers, 7 yards (grade = 0)

9:43: Dart to Singletary, 13 yards (grade = 0)

8:16: Dart to Singletary, 7 yards (grade = 0)

7:26: Dart to Singletary, 7 yards, TD (grade = 0)

4:34: Dart downfield to Nabers, incomplete (grade = -1)

4:30: Dart to Likely, 12 yards (grade = +0.5)

2:16: Dart to Likely, 5 yards (grade = +1)

OK, so how did I do? PFF said:

Positively graded plays: 32.35% of 34 dropbacks = 11 plays

My score: 9 plays

Negatively graded plays: 11.76% of 34 dropbacks = four plays

My score: 7 plays

In other words, PFF was more generous than I was in giving Dart credit for his throws in this game. I didn’t expect that, but so be it. The bottom line, which is the point of this post, is that their view of Dart’s performance against Dallas was not more critical of him than mine was. Why, then, the middling 68.5 PFF passing grade?

It’s primarily, I’m sure, because PFF values explosive plays. Ever since the Tom Brady era began, teams have been getting to and winning Super Bowls because of intermediate and deep completed passes. Teams like the 2013 Seattle Seahawks and 2015 Denver Broncos who won mainly on the basis of defense and a strong ground game have mostly been absent since then. The Giants under Dart haven’t really been that (yet). It may come in time, as Dart becomes more comfortable with Nabers, Fields, Mooney, and Odell Beckham, but for now, they are more a ”matriculate down the field” type of team.

As we can see from my attempt to grade Dart’s throws vs. PFF’s, PFF doesn’t seem to be judging Dart too harshly on whether he’s making enough good throws or not. It’s just because when you have a spray chart that looks like this:

With only two pass attempts and one completion more than 20 yards past the line of scrimmage, you’re not going to see them giving Dart a high PFF passing grade.

You may disagree that explosive plays and interceptions are important to winning and losing. Three yards and a cloud of dust was a thing when I was a kid and those didn’t matter so much. It may be quixotic of me to imagine that any amount of writing can change the way many of you look at PFF grades. I might even suggest to PFF that they could quiet some of the outrage against them by making positively and negatively graded throw percentage a standard stat they present every week. It seems that assessing +/- throws is not their problem. The problem instead seems to be getting from that to the PFF grades that we all see, which is fairly opaque.

The bottom line is that PFF in fact seems to be seeing pretty much the same thing that we all see…they are just valuing it differently. In some sense, the blame should go to Matt Nagy and Brian Callahan. If they’re designing an offense that can sustain drives and put points on the board with mostly short and intermediate pass routes that spring receivers open, who needs explosive plays? The counter-argument is that a 10-play drive has more chances to mess up and turn the ball over than a 1-play, 80-yard bomb for a TD. But the counter-counter-argument is that keeping the ball out of Dak Prescott’s hands and wearing down the opposing defense is a good game plan. You choose.

An example of another composite score for quarterbacks that gives a different result is Pro Football Sports Network’s “Impact Grade.” Impact Grade is similar to other football metrics and different from PFF’s grade in that it is based on results, not process. It doesn’t care whether a throw was difficult or easy, well thrown or lucky not to be intercepted, etc., as PFF’s grade does. It just measures what was accomplished, with a nod toward game situation so that just piling up meaningless yards is not rewarded. Impact Score uses different metrics for different positions. For QB, its metrics are

The Impact Grade starts with 75 as a “normal” score and goes up or down from there based on individual stats. For Week 1 their ranking of QBs is

That ranking will be more to the liking of BBV readers. It agrees to some extent with the PFF grades: PFSN’s top QB for Week 1, Trevor Lawrence, was PFF’s No. 2. Their No. 4, Lamar Jackson, was PFF’s No. 9. (Note, though, that the PFSN impact grade includes QB runs. The PFF grades I analyzed were just for passing. PFF also gives a QB rushing grade, and for that, Lamar was No. 1 at 81.0 and Dart No. 3 at 78.1. In total offense, which includes both, Dart’s overall PFF grade of 74.3 was 11th.)

In the end, there is probably value in noting both results and the process used to get those results. For me at least, the more metrics, the better I feel I can understand what a player is bringing to the table. The bottom line: Just win, baby.
