item.title: Steve Belichick to resign as part of UNC investigation
item.description: The move will be final after Belichick’s medical leave that began August 6.
item.content:encoded:
Steve Belichick has resigned his position of defensive coordinator at the University of North Carolina. His resignation comes after an indefinite medical leave that was announced on August 6, at the beginning of fall camp. WRAL has previously reported that an internal investigation by UNC has been asking about possible drug use by Steve Belichick in its interviews.

The son of head coach Bill Belichick, Steve came to UNC from the University of Washington, where he coached the defense under the direction of Husky head coach Jedd Fisch for one season. Prior to that stop in Seattle, Steve worked exclusively for his father and the New England Patriots for a decade.

While not unexpected, the departure of Steve Belichick continues a difficult transition to college football for head coach Bill Belichick. Bill Belichick has now seen his three most important initial hires — offensive coordinator, defensive coordinator, and general manager — either fired or resigned. In a recent press conference, Bill noted his love and concern for his child without detailing the reasons for Steve’s absence.

Since the medical leave was announced in early August, UNC has been operating without its defensive coordinator, with adjusted responsibilities among the remaining staff. In that respect, Steve’s resignation will not impact UNC’s preparations to play at Clemson on Saturday.

item.content:encoded:
Good morning, Chargers fans!

Justin Herbert’s Week One debut under new offensive coordinator Mike McDaniel likely had more eyes on it than his rookie debut back in 2020. That’s because the entire NFL world was in some way invested in finally seeing Herbert “unlocked” within a system that was supposed to take the pressure off his shoulders while also bringing back the use of his tremendous arm talent.

The things is…that didn’t happen.

At all.

Herbert and the offense looked great for one drive (their first one) and then it all came crashing down in a fiery heap of…something…for the remainder of the evening.

The team’s QB1 had some questionable decisions, including the arm punt in the fourth quarter to Derius Davis while he was double-covered. Otherwise, his teammates and him looked to be on two separate pages when it came to timing and situational awareness.

“Justin Herbert’s first game working with new offensive coordinator Mike McDaniel was rough,“ says analyst Garrett Podell. ‘‘The box score was 209 yards, a touchdown and an interception on 17-of-27 passing, but the eye test showed more troubling signs. He and his receivers — outside of Ladd McConkey — weren’t connected in terms of their timing going through progressions/routes, and his fourth-quarter interception was essentially a YOLO arm punt in which he flippantly heaved the football into double coverage near the goal line. It’s a very troubling start to Herbert’s 2026.”

item.title: Bill Belichick says speculation about Jordon Hudson's significant involvement with UNC football was 'ridiculous'
item.description: Both Belichick and the school have said that Hudson has no role within the football program.
item.content:encoded:
Bill Belichick is again saying that girlfriend Jordon Hudson has had no role with North Carolina's football program.

In an interview with the Wall Street Journal, Belichick said that he had initially asked for Hudson to be copied on his North Carolina emails shortly after he was hired because he was so busy at the start of his new job. Hudson's potential role with UNC football became the source of fascination after public records requests had unearthed Belichick's email.

In the story published Wednesday ahead of UNC's game at Clemson on Saturday, Belichick brushed off speculation of Hudson's deep involvement with the football program as "ridiculous."

From the WSJ:

"When I took the job here, it was December, and at that time I was doing five TV shows, the radio show, I had a book coming out," Belichick said. "I had a lot of other things going on when I took the job."

"So," he continued, "I sent an email when I got here and I said, Can you please forward any requests to Jordon about my personal appearances so that I can work and coordinate them outside the university? Didn't have anything to do with the university. Well, that was leaked as released as 'Jordon's involved in every single thing that I do and she's copied on every email.' That's just a flat-out lie."

Belichick went on to say that he and Hudson still have a working relationship but it's "not North Carolina stuff." The school has previously said she does not have a role with the football program. So has Belichick.

Hudson rose to prominence after Belichick was hired at North Carolina following an April 2025 interview with "CBS Sunday Morning." In it, Hudson chimed in to say that Belichick would not be answering a question about their relationship. Two weeks later, North Carolina even released a statement saying Hudson was still welcome at the team facilities — and definitely not an employee of the school — after a podcast report citing two sources that said Hudson had been told not to be at UNC's football facilities.

Recently, the off-field attention on Belichick's program has been about something much more serious. North Carolina general manager Michael Lombardi, a longtime confidant of Belichick, resigned earlier in the month amid a school investigation. Thursday, North Carolina announced that defensive coordinator Steve Belichick, Belichick’s son, would officially resign in October.

Steve Belichick had been on medical leave since before the start of the season.

Lombardi had been placed on leave pending an investigation following a complaint from a former staffer. That investigation has now reportedly been rolled into a bigger investigation that is looking into multiple aspects in the football program, reportedly including questions surrounding allegations of drug use by defensive coordinator Steve Belichick and questions about an allegation of a sexual relationship between a recruiting staffer and a player.

item.description: Bill Belichick's son, Steve Belichick, is the second high-profile resignation at UNC football, following GM Michael Lombardi earlier this season.
item.content:encoded:
North Carolina defensive coordinator Steve Belichick has resigned, following a medical leave and an investigation into the football program.

Steve Belichick, son of UNC head coach Bill Belichick, hasn't been with the team since Aug. 6 and will resign at the conclusion of his medical leave on Oct. 17, the team announced on Thursday, Sept. 17.

The abrupt resignation comes on the heels of an internal investigation, and though the investigation didn't find signs of systemic issues (per the statement), it did find "certain actions demonstrated a disregard for Carolina’s values and standards of conduct. The investigation also found that these actions were isolated in scope and not a systemic failure."

More: Bill Belichick insists he's in control at UNC. The investigation could test that claim

Opinoin: Bill Belichick has chance to accelerate Dabo Swinney downfall at Clemson

Steve Belichick follows former North Carolina GM Michael Lombardi out the door. Lombardi also resigned Sept. 3 after over a month on administrative leave during North Carolina's investigation. The school added in its statement that Belichick's resignation closes the matter and "corrective actions" will be handled in-house.

"Throughout the investigation, the University has been guided by the legal advice of outside counsel," the statement read. "All necessary corrective actions are now underway and will be overseen by Carolina Athletics and the Office of University Counsel. With these actions, the University considers the investigation to be resolved."

When it was announced Belichick was going on medical leave, Bill Belichick did not mention the investigation.

"Steve is on medical leave," Belichick had said then. "Look forward to getting him back as soon as possible."

Why did Steve Belichick resign?

Belichick's resignation came following an investigation into some of the conduct around the Bill Belichick regime. Although UNC said in its statement "disregard for Carolina’s values and standards of conduct," it is unclear what led to Steve Belichick's resignation.

Local station WRAL reported Steve Belichick was under investigation for drug use and doing drugs with players. That has not been confirmed by North Carolina.

Was Steve Belichick North Carolina coach-in-waiting?

While it was a common rumor that Bill Belichick coming to Chapel Hill was contingent on a clause that would have made his son the next UNC football head coach, that rumor was repeatedly denied by the university.

There was no indication Belichick was to be the next UNC coach.

Who will be North Carolina defensive coordinator?

Bill Belichick is expected to continue to call plays for North Carolina after getting out to a 2-0 start.

"We coach the defense collectively as a staff," Belichick said last month. "We'll continue to do that. Those coaches are involved with everybody."

It is unclear if Belichick will delegate more play-calling duties now that that situation is more permanent.

UNC football suspends WR Keeyun Chapman after arrest

In the same statement announcing Steve Belichick's resignation, the school also announced it was suspending Chapman from the team "indefinitely in connection with an incident Tuesday night."

Chapman was arrested on a misdemeanor count for carrying a concealed handgun after being involved in a traffic stop on Tuesday, Sept. 16 in Chapel Hill with a teammate.

Tar Heels wide receiver C.J. Sadler was cited for speeding, according to police reports.

"Chapman's suspension, like the actions resulting from the investigation, reflect the University's commitment to accountability and the well-being of its student athletes," the statement read. "We believe the steps announced today will help make Carolina Football a stronger program and one that continues to earn the pride of the entire Carolina community."

This story will be updated.

This article originally appeared on USA TODAY: Steve Belichick resigns as North Carolina defensive coordinator following investigation

item.title: Eagles News: Jeffery Simmons says the Titans “just need to make Jalen Hurts be a quarterback”
item.description: Philadelphia Eagles news and links for 9/17/26.
item.content:encoded:
Welcome to The Linc, the daily Philadelphia Eagles links roundup at Bleeding Green Nation!

Not sure why the Tennessee Titans, who are seven-point home underdogs on Sunday, are giving Jalen Hurts and the Eagles any bulletin board material. Especially after Philly’s starting quarterback is coming off a strong Week 1 showing. But, hey, the Birds will take it.

Let’s get to the Philadelphia Eagles news and links …

Titans star takes shot at Eagles’ Jalen Hurts before Week 2: ‘Make [him] be a QB’ – NJ.com

“We just need to make Jalen Hurts be a QB,” Jeffery Simmons said on Wednesday. “Stop his runs, make sure Hurts doesn’t get out of the pocket and make plays.” The Eagles could use these comments as bulletin-board material. What Simmons said could be taken as a jab at Hurts. Hurts has developed into a good pocket passer, but his running ability makes him even more dangerous. Hurts will have to escape Simmons’ pressure for Philadelphia’s offense to have success against the Titans. With left guard Landon Dickerson on injured reserve, second-year player Drew Kendall will likely start on Sunday. Simmons could take advantage of that matchup to get after Hurts.

Eagles Film Review: A very good defensive performance against the Commanders – BGN

The Eagles’ defense was very good against the Washington Commanders. It wasn’t an elite performance, and the final two drives left a slightly sour taste, but the unit held Jayden Daniels to 18 completions on 34 attempts for 164 yards and limited Washington to 4.4 yards per play. Given the number of new pieces in the secondary and how difficult Daniels was to defend, I came away impressed. However, this defense has an offense problem. The Eagles’ defense played 67 snaps while the offense ran only 53 and gained just 10 first downs. Washington possessed the ball for 10:02 in the fourth quarter alone and put together touchdown drives of 67 and 63 yards. You could see the defense tiring. Jalen Carter looked exhausted by the end, and the pass rush dropped off. This is becoming a familiar problem. The defense can play exceptionally well for long stretches, but asking it to keep returning to the field eventually has consequences. The advanced numbers tell an interesting story. The Eagles generated pressure on 47.4% of Washington’s dropbacks despite blitzing on only 23.7%, but Daniels was sacked just once. That matches up to the film. The rush affected him and remained disciplined, but it rarely arrived quickly. I think the Eagles were deliberately cautious because they did not want to create huge escape lanes for Daniels.

Game Review – PHI 24, WAS 22 – Iggles Blitz

OL – Not a good showing. Penalties. Sloppy blocks. Missed assignments. WAS blitzed on more than 50 percent of plays and that certainly made things tough. You also factor in a lack of game tape on a new scheme. That made it challenging to prepare. Still, the OL should have played better. Landon Dickerson wasn’t healthy and it showed. He really struggled in pass protection. He didn’t have the quickness or lateral agility to get the job done. He got some movement in the run game, but also had his share of problems on run plays. He’s now on IR. Cam Jurgens had a couple of early penalties, but I thought he was solid overall. Tyler Steen was mostly good, but he has stuff to clean up as well. Lane Johnson and Jordan Mailata were sloppier than you would want from players of their caliber. Mailata did have one highlight play.

Five thoughts on the Eagles offense: What the numbers say about Jalen Hurts vs. zone coverage, Makai Lemon’s usage – PHLY Eagles

Blocking woes aside, Lemon was not billed as a twitchy gadget player coming out of USC and is probably better utilized working the middle of the field as a slot receiver tasked with finding soft spots against zone coverage. There’s a conundrum with that, though: Lemon is a willing, but limited blocker in an offense that utilizes a heavy dose of condensed sets that will make him an important part of the run game. There were a handful of examples of him struggling in the run game in his debut, which is understandable given the transition to the league and the fact that he’s 5-foot-11, 192 pounds. Nick Cross drove Lemon into Saquon Barkley’s running lanes a couple times on Sunday and, in general, he’s not the conventional dirty-work receiver most iterations of the Kyle Shanahan-Sean McVay systems often deploy. Watching through each of the 25 routes Lemon ran against Washington, my general conclusion is that he’s still a work in progress doing most of the things the Eagles asked of him. He’s not going to consistently win against man coverage from the slot or the outside and probably shouldn’t be on the field quite as much on early downs. The best-case scenario right now is probably getting him the ball on underneath routes tied to play-action, something the Eagles didn’t utilize much against Washington and putting him in fewer blocking situations from condensed formations.

Why NFL offenses are going under center more often in 2026 – ESPN

Under center: 34% of offensive snaps. The Eagles didn’t morph into an offense from the 1980s overnight, but this 34% under-center rate was the seventh highest of any Hurts start. And the quarterback run game that faded out of the offense during the 2025 season completely evaporated. Hurts had seven carries in this game against Washington — five scrambles and two kneel-downs. There wasn’t even a tush push, as the Eagles ran Saquon Barkley, threw the ball or punted on various third- or fourth-and-2 opportunities. Barkley produced 42 yards on a third-and-2 attempt, running away from Leo Chenal, through the second level and into the open field on outside zone. His other 14 carries produced 41 yards and just five successful runs. That’s a solid performance, but it’s not the sort of 2024 Barkley the Eagles were hoping to unlock by moving toward an outside zone-heavy scheme. The same held in the passing game from under center. Hurts dropped back five times from under center. Those plays produced three incompletions, a sack and a 64-yard completion to Dontayvion Wicks on a pretty deep ball where cornerback Mike Sainristil lost track of the throw and nearly came to a complete stop in coverage. Averaging 12.8 yards per play from under center looks great in the aggregate, but the Eagles weren’t consistent in their first game under Mannion. And as the game wore on, the offense felt more like the tired, disappointing one we saw for most of 2025 than the dynamic 2024 attack. The Eagles picked up one first down in the third quarter, and it took great individual efforts to get the offense going, notably from Hurts converting a third-and-18 with his legs. It’s Week 1, and we’ll see how the offense operates in the games to come. Will we see more big plays, or will the offense struggle to move the ball consistently?

Eagles Week 2: Hurts’ legs, A.J. Brown’s absence and replacing Landon Dickerson – The Athletic

Jalen Hurts’ mobility was a major factor in Week 1. It would make sense for the Eagles to lean into Hurts’ legs this season. I’m not prepared to say it will be a prominent part of the offense because Hurts started last season averaging 44.8 yards per game in the first four games, then he reached 40 yards once the rest of the season. Yet Hurts is at his best when he can be a “triple-threat quarterback,” using his arm, mind and legs, and he’s not nearly the same quarterback if you take away that part of his skill set. Fangio acknowledged that Hurts looked quicker this summer. Hurts said when he watched this offensive system from afar, the quarterback run game “has not been an element you see.” Hurts thought his legs offer a “unique opportunity.” Mannion spoke about Hurts’ mobility from a theoretical perspective during the summer, but he saw it in action in Week 1. It’s worth wondering whether it could pique Mannion’s interest even more. “It’s a difference-maker, for sure,” Mannion said. “I know I’ve spoken about it. It’s what makes him a unique talent. It came to life in the game. You can just see how he can challenge defenses that way. He made a bunch of big plays with (his) legs. It’s certainly something that really unlocks things for us and makes him a difficult guy to defend.”

    NFL QB rankings, Week 2: Caleb Williams, Lamar Jackson and Trevor Lawrence soar into top five – NFL.com

    12) JALEN HURTS. Jalen Hurts had a classic Jalen Hurts game in Week 1, connecting on a handful of downfield shots while willing Philadelphia’s offense down the field with well-timed scrambles against Washington. The Eagles still need to be more consistent offensively on a per-play basis, but for one week, Hurts was able to carry them out of the muck to victory. Next Gen Stats insight (via NFL Pro): Hurts completed 6 of 9 downfield passes (10+ air yards) for 176 yards and three touchdowns in Week 1 against the Commanders. His yardage on those throws was the eighth-highest downfield total of his career, while he threw three-plus downfield touchdown passes for just the sixth time.

    How Drew Kendall knows he’s ready for his likely opportunity – NBCSP

    Even though Lampkin could be an option, it seems more likely that Kendall is the next man up. Whether he plays left guard or center is a different question. The Eagles could put Kendall at left guard in a 1-for-1 swap for the injured Dickerson or they could move Cam Jurgens to guard and play Kendall at his more natural spot at center. “I’ve been working with Cam,” Jalen Hurts said. “When Cam has had his off days in camp, (Kendall) steps in. But, yeah, Cam.” So maybe there’s your answer. Either way, Kendall better be ready to play on Sunday. And he thinks he is. The Eagles used a fifth-round pick to draft Kendall out of Boston College last year and he showed a major jump in his second training camp this summer. In fact, general manager Howie Roseman was interested to see how the backup interior line depth would hold up this training camp and came away impressed by what the Eagles have. Kendall is the centerpiece of that depth.

    Eagles wide receiver Hollywood Brown was ‘surprised’ by lack of playing time in Week 1 win – Inquirer

    Coach Nick Sirianni was asked about Brown’s snap count on Monday and said it will change moving forward. The Eagles coach knows the 29-year-old can create space with his speed and playmaking skills and acknowledged he’s been a decent fit in Mannion’s offense. “So, with [Sunday’s game], we have our rotations that we’re doing, you know, Hollywood could obviously help us,” Sirianni said. “We obviously want to get him into the football game because his speed is real. It just didn’t work out that way [Sunday]. … But we know that Hollywood can help us win football games, and his speed is real, and, quite frankly, just from my end, we want to get him into the football game, right?”Does it make Brown feel any better that Sirianni made those comments one day after the game? “Nah, no, it don’t,” he said. “But I’m not dwelling on it. I’m ready for next week.”

    Spadaro: Dallas Goedert does it all and does it well for the Eagles – PhiladelphiaEagles.com

    Dallas Goedert just tries to keep it simple. Mention that the tight end position in the NFL has evolved over time and he points to the idea “of doing anything they ask me to do.” Ask him about “being in a new offense” and he says that that’s kind of the nature of the NFL. “Every year, things change and you have to change with the flow of the offense,” he said. “I never get too worked up about it. I just do my job and try to execute what they want me to do on every play.”

    Are you willing to be patient with the Titans? – Music City Miracles

    The Tennessee Titans had the worst opening day imaginable. There weren’t many fans who had hope after a rough preseason, but the ones who did lost it after the 23-10 loss. It wasn’t just that they lost; it was the fact that they looked completely overmatched in every phase of the game. Robert Saleh and his staff are preaching patience. That’s easy for him to say. He has only been here for about nine months. It was just one week for him, but for those of us who have suffered through the last three seasons of Titans football, it just felt like a continuation of those dreadful years. Things don’t get any easier for Saleh and his team on Sunday. The Philadelphia Eagles are coming to Nashville on a day when the forecasted high is 98 degrees. There will probably be about 40,000 people there, and I’d wager at least 25,000 of them will be Eagles fans. The Titans will most likely be 0-2, and Saleh will be saying that it is only two weeks. How long are you willing to give them?

    NFL Power Rankings: Cardinals soar, while Packers tumble – SB Nation

    New York Giants (+7). Everything is coming up roses for the start of the John Harbaugh era in East Rutherford. This team had the raw talent on paper, but the veteran coach showed that he can harness it by dominating the Cowboys on both sides of the ball. The story moving forward will be how well Jaxson Dart can continue to play, and perhaps more-importantly, if he can stay healthy. If both those things happen we could see a very big season from the G-Men that makes a lot of noise in the NFC East.

    Giants-Rams, Week 2 preview: 5 storylines, including Aaron Donald’s return – Big Blue View

    Aaron Donald’s return? The future Hall of Fame defensive tackle, a nine-time First-Team All-Pro in 10 seasons, is back with the Rams after a two-year retirement. The 35-year-old did not make the trip to Australia with the team. Could he make his return Monday night? ”We haven’t decided that yet,” [Rams coach Sean] McVay said. “He’s going to continue to work his process and we’ll see what that looks like.” NFL Insider Ian Rapoport said there is “very, very realistic chance” Donald will be in uniform against the Giants. How much, and how well, Donald can play at this point are legitimate questions.

    Commanders vs. Cowboys Wednesday injury report: Chig Okonkwo held out – Hogs Haven

    The Commanders emerged from training camp in solid shape. While they put a few key players on injured reserve, all 53 members of the active roster were available for the regular season opener against the Philadelphia Eagles. They won’t enter Week 2 that way. A few key Commanders got banged up in that 24-22 loss to Philly, putting their status in some doubt. Tight end Chig Okonkwo (hamstring) and linebacker Frankie Luvu (groin) didn’t practice on Wednesday, the first full workout leading up to Sunday’s road test against the Dallas Cowboys.

    Cowboys injuries: DeMarvion Overshown, Malik Hooker DNP – Blogging The Boys

    Head coach Brian Schottenheimer provided some insight to injuries Monday and now we have more indication about player statuses following the Sunday’s loss. DeMarvion Overshown was designated as a DNP at Wednesday’s practice. He came up lame during Sunday night’s game and was visibly frustrated after sustaining the injury. Overshown would’ve been highly questionable to play this week with such an injury, and today’s status seems to be indicative that he is very unlikely to play this week.

    Chiefs make 5 roster moves on Wednesday – Arrowhead Pride

    Taking his place on the active roster will be [former Eagles] fullback Ben VanSumeren. VanSumeren joined Kansas City’s practice squad after final cuts. He was elevated to play against the Broncos. In his Red and Gold debut, VanSumeren was in on 79% of the Chiefs’ special teams snaps while taking the field for three offensive plays.

    Falcons put Da’Shawn Hand on IR, promote TE Nick Muse to active roster – The Falcoholic

    Muse is a former Eagle and Super Bowl LIX champion.

    The Atlanta Falcons have made it official, placing Da’Shawn Hand on injured reserve with an ailment that’s expected to knock him out for the rest of the season. The team has promoted tight end Nick Muse to the 53 man roster in a corresponding move and have added defensive end Drake Jackson and running back Khalil Herbert to the practice squad.

    Dolphins make roster moves – Miami Dolphins

    Cal Adomitis has appeared in 58 career games with Cincinnati (2022-24) and Philadelphia (2025). He also appeared in three postseason games with the Bengals. He entered the NFL as an undrafted college free agent with Cincinnati in 2022 following a five-year collegiate career at Pittsburgh (2017-21), where he appeared in 64 games and recorded 13 special teams tackles (seven solo). He finished his Pitt career as one of the most accomplished long snappers in program history, earning 2021 All-America honors and the Patrick Mannelly Award, presented to the top collegiate senior long snapper in the FBS.

item.content:encoded:
A new week is upon us as the Atlanta Falcons are preparing to host the Carolina Panthers. Following a poor performance against the Steelers, the Falcons are looking to bounce back, and for that to happen, they will need everyone to get healthy before Sunday.

Let’s take a look!

To start the week, the Falcons have a few injuries to keep an eye on. The quarterback position is still at the front of it all, as Penix Jr. was able to practice fully, but it’s reported that he may be a week or two away from feeling ready to start. Cooper Rush, who was clearly far from 100% in Week 1 despite what head coach Kevin Stefanski said, was a full participant as he heals from his back issue. Tua remains sidelined as he deals with a back injury he sustained in last week’s practice.

Some big names also started the week missing practice, as corner A.J. Terrell has a shoulder issue that he sustained during the game against the Pittsburgh Steelers. Terrell left for a few plays, and was able to return. Chris Lindstrom is unfortunately in concussion protocol so there’s no clear timeline for his return.

We will keep an eye on the health of both teams following Thursday’s practice.

item.title: Steve Belichick resigns as North Carolina defensive coordinator
item.description: Bill Belichick's son steps down amid an ongoing investigation.
item.content:encoded:
Two weeks after North Carolina G.M. Michael Lombardi abruptly resigned during an investigation regarding his conduct while working for the Tar Heels, North Carolina defensive coordinator Steve Belichick has done the same.

Via Pete Thamel of ESPN, Steve Belichick has resigned.

The son of head coach Bill Belichick, Steve has been on medical leave since August 6. No details regarding the medical condition were ever disclosed or reported.

On the day Lombardi resigned, WRAL issued a report that indicated the investigation has broadened to include Steve Belichick. Per the report, witnesses were being questioned regarding whether Steve Belichick “used drugs on the job or provided drugs to at least one player.”

There was talk when Bill Belichick took the North Carolina job that he hoped to create a succession plan that would result in Steve Belichick taking over following Bill's retirement. The contracts did not contemplate the eventual shift, and the team's performance in 2025 seemingly mooted the possibility.

Now, it definitely won't happen. The only question is whether, and when, Bill Belichick will step down.

Through it all, UNC is 2-0. It nevertheless seems as if someone (or more than one someones) at UNC are looking for an exit strategy as to the relationship with Bill Belichick, possibly through a for-cause termination that cuts off his buyout.

item.title: Browns add WR Jimmy Horn Jr. to practice squad
item.description: The Browns are adding a player who's plenty familiar with their (current) backup quarterback.
item.content:encoded:
The Browns are adding a player who's plenty familiar with their (current) backup quarterback.

According to multiple reports, Cleveland is signing receiver Jimmy Horn Jr. to its practice squad.

Horn — a Panthers sixth-round pick in last year's draft — had a rough Week 1, muffing a punt while trying to make a fair catch. He was waived earlier this week as the team added a linebacker.

Horn could help the Browns as a returner, as Dylan Sampson is expected to miss significant time with a knee injury suffered during the season-opening loss to the Jaguars.

Horn played with Shedeur Sanders at Colorado before both were drafted last year. With Deshaun Watson struggling through Cleveland's season opener as QB1, Sanders could be elevated to a starting role sooner than later.

item.title: Arizona Cardinals Daily Links: Cardinals shoot up power rankings after upset victory
item.description: The Cardinals went from 25th to 19th in NFL.com’s latest NFL power rankings.
item.content:encoded:
The Cardinals were underdogs by more than a touchdown against the Chargers, but that didn’t stop them from winning in Week One by double-digits.

After that impressive victory, the Cardinals saw themselves shoot up numerous power rankings this week, including going from 25th to 19th in Nick Shook’s rankings at NFL.com.

Here’s what he had to say about the Cardinals and their ranking:

“The upset of the week belongs to Arizona, a team most everyone counted out in the opener at Los Angeles. As it turns out, we were all wrong; Mike LaFleur’s group played inspired, fearless football, taking the fight to the Chargers and outplaying them in every facet. Enjoy the triumphant debut, Cardinals fans.”

Do you think this is the correct ranking for the Cardinals after just one win? Should they be higher? Lower? Let us know in the comments below!

item.title: Titans need way more from John Franklin-Myers in Week 2
item.description: Tennessee Titans defensive lineman John Franklin-Myers was totally ineffective in the Week 1 loss to the Jets
item.content:encoded:
Several new Tennessee Titans players failed to meet expectations in Sunday’s Week 1 loss to the New York Jets. One of the glaring ones was defensive tackle John Franklin-Myers. The Titans need Franklin-Myers to be way better versus the Philadelphia Eagles in Week 2.

The Titans signed Franklin-Myers to a three-year, $63 million contract in free agency. That’s a hefty deal to play next to Jeffery Simmons. Franklin-Myers was brought in for his experience in Robert Saleh’s system, having played under him with the Jets.

Remember that Franklin-Myers missed a huge portion of training camp with stiffness and soreness. The former Stephen F. Austin standout did not play a single snap in the preseason. Franklin-Myers got the veteran rest treatment, but it clearly had a negative impact on his Week 1 performance.

Franklin-Myers recorded just three tackles and one quarterback pressure against the Jets. Pro Football Focus slapped him with an overall defensive grade of 52.7. His PFF pass-rushing grade was a 52.8, and run-stopping score wasn’t much better (55.4). Franklin-Myers was totally ineffective.

The Eagles are dealing with an injury on the offensive line. They’ll be without starting left guard Landon Dickerson, who is a Pro Bowl-caliber interior blocker. The expectation is that sophomore backup Drew Kendall will replace him. Both Simmons and Franklin-Myers need to take advantage of that matchup.

The Titans paid Franklin-Myers very handsomely to be a dominant force on the defensive line. His impact was totally muted by an underrated Jets offensive line in Week 1. Nonetheless, Coach Saleh’s defensive line was very disappointing. Franklin-Myers needs to help lead the charge towards improvement.

The Titans have had way too many big-money flops lately. They certainly can’t afford another. It’s obviously far too early to panic. Franklin-Myers is known as a consistent defensive lineman. Hopefully Franklin-Myers will perform like his usual self soon.

item.title: Jaguars vs Broncos: Matchup History Through the Decades
item.description: The Jaguars and Broncos have played each other 16 times, and the series is currently tied.
item.content:encoded:
The current AFC South Division leaders, the Jacksonville Jaguars, will be on the road for Week 2 to face off against the Denver Broncos. The Jaguars and Broncos series is tied 8-8. Experts do not like the Jags’ odds, but here’s hoping they deliver the upset two seasons in a row and take the series lead while we revisit Jacksonville in Denver through the decades.

The 1990s

AFC Divisional Playoff at Mile High Stadium on January 4, 1997
Final score: Jaguars 30 – Broncos 27
Attendance: 75,678

The Jaguars recorded 22 first downs, 443 total net yards, and a 32:24 time of possession, compared to the Broncos’ 21 first downs, 351 total net yards, and 27:36 time of possession. Natrone Means, Keenan McCardell, and Jimmy Smith scored touchdowns. Mark Brunell completed 18 out of 29 attempted passes for 245 yards and was sacked twice for a loss of five yards. Natrone Means led the team with 140 rushing yards, and Jimmy Smith led with 71 receiving yards. Mike Hollis made the three attempted field goals. Eddie Robinson registered a sack on John Elway.

The 2000s

Week 3 at Invesco Field at Mile High on September 23, 2007
Final score: Jaguars 23 – Broncos 14
Attendance: 76,463

Reggie Williams and Greg Jones scored touchdowns. David Garrard completed 14 out of 20 attempted passes for 154 yards and was sacked three times for a loss of 14 yards. Fred Taylor led the team with 84 rushing yards, and Marcedes Lewis led with 44 receiving yards. John Carney made the three attempted field goals. Sammy Knight had an interception, and Reggie Hayward recorded a sack on Jay Cutler for a loss of four yards.

The 2010s

Week 4 on September 29, 2019, at Empower Field at Mile High
Final Score: Jaguars 26 – Broncos 24
Attendance: 76,219

Ryquell Armstead and James O’Shaughnessy scored the Jaguars’ two touchdowns during the third quarter. Minshew completed 19 out of 33 attempted passes for 213 yards and was sacked five times for a loss of 27 yards. Leonard Fournette was on fire with 225 rushing yards, and Dede Westbrook led the team with 66 receiving yards. Lambo made the four attempted field goals. Jarrod Wilson and Quincy Williams led the team with eight combined tackles each.

The 2020s

Week 16 on December 21, 2025, at Empower Field at Mile High
Final Score: Jaguars 34 – Broncos 20
Attendance: 76,858

The two teams traded punts during the first quarter, until the Broncos decided to go for it on fourth down and get the needed yardage for a field goal. Unfortunately for them, Lutz’s kick hit the uprights. The Jaguars’ offense started cooking, leading to a Parker Washington touchdown. The Broncos started the second quarter striking back with a touchdown by Sutton and a field goal by Lutz to bring Denver’s lead to 10-7. Strange puts another seven on the board for Jacksonville, and following a punt by the Broncos, Cam Little increases the lead by three. The second half starts with the two teams trading touchdowns. With roughly four minutes left in the third quarter, the offense scores again for Jacksonville. The Broncos try to decrease the deficit but fumble the ball, and the Jags recover. Little’s kick is good to increase the lead to 34-17. Denver kicks a field goal, and Jarrian Jones intercepts the ball during their next drive. The Jags succeed with the upset.

item.title: Saints vs. Ravens: Quarterback Matchup
item.description: Saints and Tyler Shough will face off against former league MVP in Lamar Jackson and the Ravens
item.content:encoded:
The Saints are back on the road again following the loss in Detroit, and the matchup is not getting any easier. The Saints have to travel up to Baltimore and line up across from a two-time MVP in Lamar Jackson.

Jackson has a new head coach in Jesse Minter and a new OC in Declan Doyle. Doyle was an assistant under Sean Payton from 2019-2022 and then went with Payton to Denver for the 2023 and 2024 seasons as well. He was promoted to OC under Ben Johnson last season with the Chicago Bears, but now he is serving as the play caller for Minter in Baltimore, and it seems like that was a great move.

Baltimore and Jackson were unlocked last week in Indianapolis against the Colts. Jackson finished the game 17/25 for 324 yards, 13 yards per attempt, one passing touchdown, 40 rushing yards, and one rushing touchdown with no turnovers.

If Doyle can make Jackson a more efficient passer of the football, this will definitely cause problems for the rest of the league, especially considering the balance that the offense has with Derrick Henry still being able to run the ball effectively.

The Saints are going to have their hands full with Jackson at QB. He’s becoming a more patient passer, but he’s still just as dangerous as a runner. His speed and quickness are second to none, and his vision with the ball makes him as elusive as a running back in the open field. This will not be an easy challenge.

Overall, the Saints defense did not play poorly against Detroit. The offense put them in some very tough situations, and in the third quarter, it did so rather quickly with back-to-back turnovers. Hopefully, those issues get cleaned up this week.

That leads us into Tyler Shough.

Shough is coming off one of the most impressive second-half performances the Saints have seen in quite some time. Shough finished the game last week with 410 passing yards on 35/56 completions for a completion percentage of 62.5%. He had three touchdowns, but he also had two interceptions and a fumble.

It was literally a tale of two halves for Shough.

It was not until the Saints went down 21-0 in the third quarter that this young, budding star turned the lights on and absolutely went off. Shough finished the second half 25/34 for a 73.5% completion percentage with three touchdowns, leading the Saints to score 30 points.

That is a franchise-level performance for a half of football.

But the Saints and this offense need to come out faster than this. In this game, on the road in Baltimore against a defense that will look to be aggressive, starting slow could potentially bury the Saints.

The Saints did not fare too well against Aidan Hutchinson last week, and the Ravens added Trey Hendrickson over the offseason to bolster their pass rush. Not only that, but they also have a really good corner in Nate Wiggins who can match up with Chris Olave.

Shough will have to be consistent from start to finish if the Saints are going to pull off this upset. Right now, the Ravens are favored by 8.5 points to win the game. It is a tall task, but upsets happen every day in the NFL.

How do you think the Saints match up at the QB position, and do you think they can pull off this upset?

item.title: Cowboys roundtable discussion: What to look for in Commanders game
item.description: Here is our latest roundtable with a panel of BTB writers giving us their answers to this week’s questions
item.content:encoded:
Every week, we gather to discuss the latest news about the Dallas Cowboys and seek our writer’s perspective on each headline. Welcome back to the roundtable. This week we have Jorge Guajardo, DyllanRivers, Tom Ryle and Sean Martin. 

What was the biggest problem that the Cowboys had against the Giants in opening week?

MIKE: Dallas’ biggest issue was the defense not getting off the field. The Cowboys allowed 9-of-11 third-down conversions, missed seven tackles, gave up 165 combined rushing yards, and let Jaxson Dart finish 23-of-29 with three touchdowns. The Giants also controlled the ball for nearly 37 minutes, which shaped the whole game and kept the Cowboys offense off the field. That all boils down to one issue, the defense playing efficient football, very simple. 

JORGE: The defense is still really bad, and the effort and attention to detail were poor in Week 1. Four Cowboys linebackers- Winters, Overshown, Houston and Lawrence were given PFF grades between 34 and 42. 

DYLLAN: The Giants tried their best to serve up five turnovers. Dallas only accepted one of those gifts. On a night where the defense allowed the Giants to methodically move down the field and chew up clock, those turnovers would have gone a long way in turning the tide.

SEAN: Not winning at the point of attack, or getting in on a record-breaking Sunday elsewhere around the league for offense despite the expectations on that side of the ball. The Giants brain trust on offense is way too experienced now to not expect them to dominate the game if they’re not worried about negative plays or pass rush, and that’s exactly what happened as the Giants imposed their will up front. The possessions for the offense were limited by this, every mistake was magnified as a result, and when even veteran players like Javonte Williams make that list for critical mistakes, it’s asking a whole lot to win on the road against anyone in this league. Humble pie was served, Jersey diner style.

TOM: Let’s take an overhead view and say that Brian Schottenheimer and his staff just got pantsed by John Harbaugh and crew. They had a plan and carried it out very well, with only the sloppiness with the ball to really mar things. They mocked the defense, stymied the offense, and just looked like a team that was miles and miles ahead in preparation and motivation.

What’s the biggest improvement you want to see this Sunday against Washington?

MIKE: The biggest improvement has to be defensive discipline, especially on third down. Against the Giants, Dallas kept giving New York manageable situations, then failed to finish drives with stops. That cannot happen against Washington and Jayden Daniels, because if the rush lanes get sloppy or the tackling is loose, he can turn broken plays into back-breakers.

JORGE: Removing excuses. Cleaning up the miscues, making adjustments and upping the effort will be vital to properly assess this team’s deficiencies, particularly on defense.  

DYLLAN: Physicality up front. Our defensive tackles are too good to be bullied in the middle of the field. And let us see the outside guys stay home to set the edge instead of consistently crashing down, leaving a void for the mobile QB to take advantage of.

SEAN: Running the ball better. Since Dan Quinn has been in Washington, Cowboys fans haven’t been shy talking about the deficiencies in the Commanders run defense, which were of course an issue when Quinn was here as well. Be it by better defense or a better run game, the Cowboys need to show more around Dak Prescott for it not to be all on his shoulders like it was Sunday night, and I have more faith in Javonte Williams plus the offensive line in this game than I do the defense improving much right now.

TOM: Could we get more third down stops. Oh, wait, given that they only had two all game, how about just getting more than one a half? Admittedly, the Cowboys were almost as good at converting, but with the way the Giants controlled the ball and the clock, this was one of the bigger nails in the coffin.

Dallas was hurt by penalties and missed chances in Week 1. Is discipline still the biggest concern with this team?

MIKE: Think this goes without saying, discipline is still the biggest concern. Penalties, missed tackles, blown assignments and wasted chances all feed into the same issue, Dallas is making the game harder than it needs to be. Against the Giants, it was not just that mistakes happened, it was when they happened. Drives were extended, field position was lost, and the Cowboys failed to cash in moments where they could have taken control.

JORGE: I would say discipline and focus are monumental concerns. George Pickens’ drops and the lack of detail and care on the defensive side are key indicators of that. The Giants ended up with more penalties and yards by game’s end, but the Cowboys’ penalty timing is still really bad.

DYLLAN: Overall discipline is still a concern. From penalties to individual responsibilities, the players just weren’t ready. Too many dropped passes, untimely penalties, and leaving plays on the field. This needs to be quickly corrected to avoid 0-2.

SEAN: I actually don’t think so. Clearly the Cowboys had moments where they were undisciplined in this loss, but I see it as more under the umbrella of just being outcoached. Players were not put in the best position to win compared to the Giants.

TOM: Dallas has had a real problem with excessive penalties for years now, and to me, that just screams undisciplined play. It is a hard pill to swallow given how much talk there was about culture building, but there is still so very far to go.

item.title: 5 Questions with the Enemy: Asking a Giants fan what makes Jaxson Dart special as he begins his sophomore season
item.description: “He can make plays with his legs, and there is some magic when he is off-script, says Big Blue View of Dart
item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Rams look to rebound in Week 2 with a home date against the upstart New York Giants. New York is 1-0 under new head coach John Harbaugh, whose team appears to be a much tougher opponent than previously thought.

Much of the Giants’ success in the season opener is due to second-year quarterback Jaxson Dart. The Ole Miss product looks to build on a promising start to his NFL career. This week, I spoke with Giants writer Ed Valentine from Big Blue View to learn more about Dart, the culture under Harbaugh and more.

Q – The John Harbaugh era kicked off in style with a 28-20 win over the Cowboys on Sunday night. What are your early impressions of the Harbaugh era thus far, and how do you expect the Giants to fare in his first season?

A – John Harbaugh is the right coach at the right time for the Giants. He has brought credibility and set a standard of expectation for everyone in the organization that the Giants badly needed. I think eight or nine wins is fair. Remember, this team won just seven games combined the last two seasons.

Q – Jaxson Dart had an excellent game against Dallas in Week 1, throwing three touchdown passes and adding 54 rushing yards. What are his strengths and possible weaknesses that the Rams’ defense could exploit, even with Myles Garrett out?

A – Dart is tough. He is unafraid. He is smart. He can make plays with his legs, and there is some magic when he is off-script. He is still a young quarterback, though, and he doesn’t always see everything correctly. Case in point: the sack/fumble Sunday when he was hit by Caleb Downs on a blitz. There was no blocker for Downs, and it was the QB’s responsibility to see that blitzer and get the ball out. Dart didn’t see it, and nearly turned the ball over.

Q – New York played smashmouth football in the opener, rushing for 165 yards and a touchdown on 37 carries. If you were Chris Shula, how would you limit the damage of the Giants’ physical rushing attack?

A – First of all, tell his guys to buckle. The Giants will be physical. They come at you with a 300-pound fullback, a running back who lives to run through people, and an attitude that they will run the football and win the line of scrimmage.

The Giants did what they wanted offensively against the Cowboys. They ran it when they wanted to. They threw it when they wanted to. I think teams will eventually opt to crowd the line of scrimmage.

Q – Who are some offensive standouts LA fans should keep an eye on this week? What about on defense?

A – Offense — If you watched on Sunday, you know how important tight end Isaiah Likely is for Dart. He is what I call the “gotta have it” guy. That’s where Dart wants to go when the Giants have to have a play. 

I’m curious if RB Najee Harris has a role after being inactive in Week 1. And, of course, there is a guy named Beckham who did not get a target in Week 1. I think that will change on Monday.

Defense — Arvell Reese, the No. 5 overall pick in the draft, had a quiet game against the Cowboys. He won’t be quiet forever. I also think Abdul Carter, last year’s No. 3 overall pick, is going to have a huge season.

Q – The Giants are 7.5-point underdogs at FanDuel Sportsbook. What is your prediction for this game?

A – I think the Rams win, but this Giants team is no pushover. As I answer this, the line is 7.5. I’d take the Giants with the points.

item.title: Packers Film Room: Week 1 pressure of the week
item.description: Breaking down the creeper pressure that led to Edgerrin Cooper’s 4th quarter sack.
item.content:encoded:
In the last article, we covered the week 1 blitz of the week. In this article we’ll cover the pressure of the week. The difference between two is simple, a blitz sends five or more rushers at the quarterback.

A pressure can be generated without a blitz and it can involve simulated pressures and creeper pressures. Pressure is also loosely something used to describe what happens to a quarterback as soon as he’s throwing the ball (a hit, hurry, or sack).

Creeper and sim pressures are ways defenses disguise pressure by sending different rushers than the front initially shows, while dropping a would-be rusher into coverage — keeping the same number of rushers (usually four) as a standard down, but changing who’s doing the rushing.

Simulated pressure

A sim pressure shows blitz-like pressure — often with multiple defenders walked up near the line — but ultimately rushes a “normal” number of players (typically four), just not the four the offense expects.

The defense drops a lineman or an edge player into coverage and replaces him with a blitzing linebacker or defensive back. It’s designed to confuse protection (it simulates a blitz look pre-snap and alters the offensive line slide protection without actually bringing extra numbers). It creates free access or leverage against the protection’s blocking rules.

Creeper pressure

A creeper is closely related but usually refers more specifically to bringing an off-ball defender (linebacker or DB) while dropping a down lineman or edge rusher into a shallow coverage zone (often a “spy” or hook/curl zone).

The name comes from the rusher “creeping” up late or from depth rather than lining up on the line pre-snap, making it harder for the quarterback and O-line to identify pre-snap. Creepers tend to emphasize disguise and late movement more than the wholesale front-to-coverage swap that defines a sim pressure.

In practice, the two terms overlap a lot in modern usage (Fangio-tree defenses especially), and people often use “sim” as the umbrella term with “creeper” as a specific flavor of it — a same-number pressure where the exchange rusher comes from depth or off the ball rather than off the edge.

Wasp creeper

“Wasp” is a simulated pressure to the weak side that attacks the A-gap with the Jack linebacker. In Fangio’s terminology, of which Jonathan Gannon is a part of, the “Jack” refers to the linebacker most teams would call the Will, or weak-side ILB.

On Wasp, the Jack linebacker shoots the A-gap on his side while the Nose occupies the A-gap on the opposite side or the center.

If the offense lines up 3×1, the defense rotates into a strong-side Cover 3; if it’s a 2×2 look instead, the defense plays Quads (Quarters) coverage, which has the option to bracket down into Palms (2-Read).

Facing a 3×1 double-slot alignment, the defense calls Wasp paired with cover-3 behind it. The offense counters with four verticals, a concept designed to attack the weaknesses in cover-3.

Here, the Vikings motion from a 2-back back field (the 3×1 side) to a 2×2 just before the snap. The coverage most likely would have shifted from cover-3 to quarters here.

At the second level, the Safeties will read the release of the tight end and opposite #2 receiver. If the tight end releases, like he does here, the safety will get over the top of a potential vertical. If the tight end were to stay in and block, there’s no more vertical threat and the safeties would redirect their eyes to the far side to wall off any crossing routes.

The routes barely develop here as linebacker Edgerrin Cooper sprints through the A-gap and sacks Carson Wentz as he barely hits the top of his dropback, forcing a 6-yard loss. Cooper gets a free run thanks to the nose tackle and defensive tackle occupying the center and left guard.

Unfortunately on this drive, the very next play resulted in an illegal contact penalty after Wentz was sacked by Cooper and Devonte Wyatt. A couple of ticky-tack penalties called on the Packers defense kept this drive alive and moving down the field until the Vikings eventually scored what would end up being the game-winning points.

item.title: Opponent Breakdown: SMU Mustangs Defense
item.description: SMU isn’t known for its defense, but Rhett Lashlee has to be happy about how his group has started this season. The Mustangs have been very stingy against the pass, while also making plenty of plays against the run to slow down opposing offenses. This defense had to replace a lot of its top contributors […]
item.content:encoded:
SMU isn’t known for its defense, but Rhett Lashlee has to be happy about how his group has started this season. The Mustangs have been very stingy against the pass, while also making plenty of plays against the run to slow down opposing offenses. This defense had to replace a lot of its top contributors from last year, but they have not fallen off, and they will present some specific challenges for Jeff Brohm and his offense.

Aakil Washington leads the group up front on the defensive line. The defensive end has been around the ball a lot when you watch this defense play, and he has 4 pressures through two games. He and Ira Singleton man the edges of this 4-2-5 scheme, while Malcolm Alcorn-Warner is the main player in the middle with 10 pressures this year.

Louisville has not been good enough on the offensive line so far this year, but this is a solid matchup for them on paper. SMU has decent size with two 300-pound tackles, but they are not as athletic as Ole Miss was up front. If they can hold serve against this front, we could see the running game unlock some things this weekend.

Linebacker is a strong group for SMU, with Alexander Kilgore being a key returner for the defense. The veteran linebacker teams up with Brandon Booker as the leaders of this defense that did not return a lot of players from last season. These two players are so valuable to this defense because they have been in it for a while, and they can make the calls and adjustments. This defense isn’t built for these guys to make a lot of tackles, but it will be interesting to see if they have the linebackers play downhill like we’ve seen so far this year to try to slow down Isaac Brown.

The secondary is the key in this defensive scheme, with the safeties leading the team in tackles last season, and this year’s group doing the same. The Mustangs play an aggressive scheme with their safeties getting downhill to support the run. They also funnel the passing game into the middle of the field with the expectation that they will have people there to make tackles on quick throws.

This defense wants to get their defensive ends in the backfield and their safeties up the field to support the run. UofL will need to avoid negative plays and take advantage of this rebuilt secondary. There is some inexperience in this group as well as a couple of guys who transferred in from G6 schools. The Cards could have an edge here.
